en: The Sūtra of Golden Light;
the Sovereign King of the Supreme Sūtras of Golden Light.
The Chapter on the Introduction.
Oṃ, homage to all the glorious Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Blessed Lady, the Noble Prajñāpāramitā! It is as follows:
Oṃ, svāhā to the victory over hearing, memory, movement, and understanding!
In which the ten supreme perfections are indicated by various methods,
and the ten stages (bhūmis) have been proclaimed for the benefit of the world by the Omniscient One;
and the stainless middle way, free from annihilation and permanence, has been declared as the goal.
Let those who seek awakening listen to that Sūtra spoken by Suvarṇaprabha.
I have heard that at one time the Tathāgata was on Vulture Peak.
He dwelt in the profound realm of phenomena, the sphere of the Buddhas.
by the great family deity Bodhisattvasamuccayā, by the great deity Sarasvatī,
and by the great deity Śrī;

Together with the great earth goddess Dṛḍhā, the great goddess Hārītī, and other such great goddesses, as well as many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what will their Dharma and Vinaya be?
The Blessed One replied with verses:
And this cultivation of the stainless samādhi, which is the essence of the Dharma and firmly established, was taught through difficult questions concerning the pure,
stainless, and supreme Bodhisattvas;
it is this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of sūtras, the primary cause [of their attainment].
Then, through the hearing of the profound and the profound investigation [of it],
the Buddhas established their empowerment throughout the four directions.
Akṣobhyarāja is in the east; by Ratnaketu in the south;
Amitābha in the west; and Dundubhisvara in the north. (Suv 1.4)
I shall proclaim that supreme empowerment, the most excellent teaching of auspiciousness,
which serves to destroy all evils and brings about the exhaustion of all misdeeds.
The bestower of all happiness, the destroyer of all suffering,
the root of the reality of omniscience, and adorned with every glory.
For those beings whose faculties are impaired, who are ruined and have lost their life-span, who are indeed surrounded by misfortune and have turned their backs on the deities; Suv_1.7 //
Those people are hated by their beloved ones, driven from their households and so forth,
or they are mutually opposed and afflicted by the loss of wealth.

In times of grief, exhaustion, misfortune, fear, and calamity; during afflictions caused by planets and constellations, or by *kākhorda* spells and terrible planetary influences; [in these states, one should recite this mantra].
One who has seen a bad dream, characterized by an abundance of grief and exhaustion,
should listen to this supreme sūtra after having purified themselves by bathing.
Those who hear this profound sūtra, the domain of the Buddhas, with clear minds and joyful hearts, adorned in clean garments; Suv_1.11 //
For all those beings, all such extremely terrible calamities are constantly pacified for all living creatures by the power of this sūtra.
The world-protectors themselves, together with their ministers and the lords of their hosts,
will provide protection for them along with many tens of millions of yakṣas.
The great goddess Sarasvatī, as well as she who dwells by the Nairañjanā,
Hārītī the mother of spirits, and the firm earth-deity.
Together with the Brahmās and Indras, the lords of the thirty-three gods, the kinnara lords of great supernatural power, the garuḍa lords, as well as the yakṣas, gandharvas, and pannagas.
Having approached that place together with their armies, forces, and vehicles,
they will provide protection for them, day and night, with focused minds. (Suv 1.16)
I shall proclaim this sūtra, the profound domain of the Buddhas,
the secret of all Buddhas, difficult to encounter even in ten million eons.
Those who hear this sutra, and others who cause it to be heard, those who rejoice in it, and those who indeed offer worship— Suv_1.18.
They shall indeed be honored for many tens of millions of eons by gods,
nāgas, humans, kinnaras, asuras, and guhyakas.
The mass of merit of those living beings who have performed meritorious deeds is boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable, as it extends forth.
They will be upheld by all the Buddhas of the ten directions,
and likewise by Bodhisattvas of profound conduct.
Having put on clean robes and purified with fragrant water,
one should, having aroused a mind of loving-kindness, worship without indolence.
He will cultivate a vast and stainless mind as his very self;
with hearts full of serene confidence, listen to this supreme sūtra.
Welcome to those among human beings who have well-obtained the fruit of humanity;
they live their lives well who listen to this sutra. (Suv 1.24)
Those into whose ear-cavity this teaching enters have planted roots of merit and have been illuminated by many Buddhas. (Suv 1.25)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsottama.
(Bagchi 4) // Chapter on the Exposition of the Lifespan of the Tathāgata //

Furthermore, at that time and on that occasion, there lived in the great city of Rājagṛha a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ruciraketu, who had performed services for previous Victors, planted roots of merit, and attended upon many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
This thought occurred to him:
"What is the cause, what is the condition, that the lifespan of the Blessed One Śākyamuni is so short, namely eighty years? Then this occurred to him:
"And it has been said by the Blessed One that there are two causes and two conditions for long life."
Which two? Abstaining from taking life and providing food.

Then, for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons, the Blessed One Śākyamuni abstained from taking life, until he had caused others to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action.
Meanwhile, the Blessed One had relinquished internal food as well as external objects for the sake of sentient beings;
indeed, even his own body—flesh, blood, bone, and marrow—had been used to satisfy hungry beings, let alone other kinds of food.
Then, as that man contemplated this very thought while maintaining the mental recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), his house became vast and spacious.
A body of the Tathāgata, made of beryl and inlaid with many divine jewels, appeared, suffused with a fragrance surpassing that of the divine realms.
And in that house, in the four directions, four seats made of divine jewels manifested;
upon those seats, divine couches were manifested, arranged with flowers and petals of divine jewels.
Upon those couches, there appeared divine lotuses inlaid with many jewels, bearing the forms of Tathāgatas.
And upon those lotuses, four Blessed Buddhas appeared:
to the east appeared the Tathāgata Akṣobhya; to the south appeared the Tathāgata Ratnaketu; to the west appeared the Tathāgata Amitāyus; and to the north appeared the Tathāgata Dundubhisvara.
They appeared;
and as soon as those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, had appeared upon those lion-thrones,
at that very moment the great city of Rājagṛha was illuminated and pervaded by a vast radiance.

As far as the trichiliocosm—the great trichiliocosm world-system—and as far as the world-systems in the ten directions, equal in number to the sands of the river Ganges, were filled with that radiance.
Celestial flowers rained down, and celestial musical instruments resounded.
And by the power of the Buddha, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm became endowed with celestial happiness.
Beings who were blind from birth saw forms; beings who were deaf heard sounds from other beings;
and beings who were insane regained their mindfulness and became possessed of undistracted minds and memory.
Naked beings became clothed in robes;
hungry beings had their bodies fully nourished;
and thirsty beings were freed from thirst.

Beings afflicted by disease became free from disease; beings with impaired bodies had their faculties restored to fullness. In detail, many marvelous and extraordinary phenomena appeared in the world.
Then, indeed, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ruciraketu, having seen those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, was struck with wonder.

Thinking, "How can this be? he became satisfied, uplifted, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; bowing with palms joined toward where those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were, he remained there recollecting those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Blessed One.
Recalling the virtues of Śākyamuni, having fallen into doubt regarding the lifespan of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, he remained there reflecting upon that very thought:
"How can this be?"
"Why is it that the lifespan of the Blessed One Śākyamuni is so short, namely eighty years?
Then those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, being mindful and clearly conscious, said this to the Bodhisattva Ruciraketu:
"Do not think thus, noble son, that the lifespan of the Blessed One Śākyamuni is so short."
For what reason? Indeed, noble son, we do not perceive anyone in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins,
including gods, humans, and asuras, who would be capable of reaching the limit of the lifespan of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

Until the furthest limits of the future, excluding only the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas; immediately upon those Blessed Buddhas having uttered this exposition on the measure of the Tathāgata’s lifespan,
by the power of the Buddha, the sons of the gods of the desire realm and the form realm assembled, as did the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
And many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas had gathered in the house of that bodhisattva Ruciraketu.
Then those Tathāgatas addressed the entire assembly with verses concerning the exposition of the lifespan of the Blessed One Śākyamuni:
"It might be possible to count all the drops of water in every ocean."
But the lifespan of Śākyamuni cannot be calculated anywhere.
It might be possible to reduce Mount Sumeru to atoms and to calculate them by number,
but it is never possible to calculate the lifespan of the Śākya-muni.
Whatever earths there may be, and however many atoms there exist— it might be possible to count them all, but not the lifespan of the Victor. (Suv 2.3)
If someone should wish to measure space by any means whatsoever, it might be possible;
but the lifespan of the Śākya-muni can never be calculated anywhere.
Thus he has remained for eons and hundreds of millions of eons; indeed, this Perfectly Awakened One cannot be measured by calculation.
For there are two causes for that, and likewise two conditions:
abstaining from harming others and giving much food.
Because the number of years of that Great Being’s lifespan cannot be found;
thus have the eons been described, yet they are not even comparable in number.
Therefore, O sir, have no doubt; do not entertain any doubt at all.
No limit to the lifespan of the Jina can ever be found.

Then, at that time, in that assembly, a brahmin named Kauṇḍinya, who had received the prophecy of a master, together with many thousands of brahmins, having performed acts of worship for the Blessed One and hearing the news of the Tathāgata’s great parinirvāṇa, suddenly rose, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One in this way:

"O Blessed One, if indeed you are compassionate toward all beings, possessed of great mercy, seeking the welfare of all beings, acting as a mother and father to all beings, being unequaled and equal to all, like the moon, creating light, and having arisen like the sun of great wisdom and knowledge— if you regard Rāhula as your own son, grant me one boon. The Blessed One remained silent.
Then, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, a Licchavi youth named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, who was present in that assembly,
was inspired with eloquence.
He spoke thus to the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, who had received the prophecy from the Teacher:
"Why do you, Great Brahmin, ask the Blessed One for only one boon?
I shall grant you a boon.
The Brahmin said:
"O Litsavi prince,
for the purpose of honoring and attending upon the Blessed One, I desire to deposit a relic of the Blessed One the size of a mustard seed;
having honored this relic the size of a mustard seed for my own purpose, [I shall attain] the sovereignty of the Tridaśa gods."
"It is heard that it is thus obtained.

Listen, Prince Liṭsaviku, to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which is difficult for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to understand. Indeed, one who is endowed with such marks and qualities shall practice this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*."
"Thus, O Prince Litsavikumāra, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is difficult to understand and difficult to realize.
For us Brahmins of the borderlands, it is more appropriate to preserve a relic the size of a mustard seed placed within a casket.
I ask you for a boon by which sentient beings may quickly attain the sovereignty of the Thirty-three Gods."

"O Prince Litsavi, you indeed desire to request from me a relic of the Tathāgata the size of a mustard seed; by placing that relic in a jewel casket and wearing it, you wish for all sentient beings to obtain the sovereignty of the Lord of the Thirty-three. Such was the boon desired by me, Prince Litsavi."
Then the Licchavi youth named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana addressed the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, who had received the prophecy from the Teacher, with these verses:
"When lotuses grow in the currents of the Gaṅgā,
when crows become red, and when cuckoos take on the color of conch shells."
If one should give a rose-apple, a palmyra fruit, a date, or a mango blossom,
then even a quantity the size of a mustard seed will clearly become a precious metal.
When he is well-covered with cloaks made of tortoise hair,
then the element will ward off the cold during the winter.
When even the legs of mosquitoes become a support for a palace—
firm and unshakable— then the relics will appear.
When sharp, large, and white teeth grow for all the leeches, then their mineral essence will appear. (Suv_2.13)
When a ladder made of rabbit horns becomes perfectly firm for the purpose of ascending to heaven, only then will there be a creator.
When a mouse climbs that ladder, devours the moon,
and runs all around Rāhu, then the Dharma-body will come to pass.
When flies wandering through the village, having drunk from a jar of wine,
shall make their dwelling in a house, then the relics will appear.
When the donkey, endowed with lips as red as the *bimba* fruit, becomes happy in dancing and singing, then the relics will be well.
For when owls and crows come together and sport with one another in harmony, then the Dharma-king will appear.
When a vast canopy of palāśa leaves appears,
then the relics will be protected from the falling rain.
When ocean-going ships, equipped with machinery and adorned with banners,
should travel by ascending onto dry land, then the Dharma-teacher will appear.
For when owls should take up Mount Gandhamādana with their beaks and carry it away, then the time of the Teacher will have come.
Having heard these verses, the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, who had received the prophecy from the Teacher, replied in verse to the prince Litsavikumāra, who was beloved by all the world:
"Excellent, excellent, O foremost of princes, son of the Conqueror, you of great voice!
You are a hero skilled in means, having attained the supreme prophecy. (Suv 2.22)
"Listen, my son, to the inconceivable majesty of the Protector of the World, the Tathāgata, in its proper sequence."
The domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable, and the Tathāgatas are peerless;
all Buddhas are eternally auspicious, and all Buddhas are identical in their conduct.
All Buddhas are of equal nature; this is the true nature of the Buddhas.
That Blessed One is not artificial, nor has the Tathāgata ever arisen.
His body is of adamantine composition, yet he manifests emanated bodies;
even for the great seers, there is not so much as a mustard-seed-sized relic to be found. (Suv 2.26)
When the body is without bones or blood, how can there be any relic?
The deposition of relics is a skillful means for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
For the Dharmakāya is the Perfectly Awakened One, and the Dharmadhātu is the Tathāgata;
such is the body of the Blessed One, and such is his teaching of the Dharma.
Having heard this and understood it, I requested a boon;
for the sake of the explanation of reality, I brought about the arising of the boon from the Sage.

Then, indeed, thirty-two thousand sons of the gods, having heard this profound teaching on the measure of the Tathāgata’s lifespan, all conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; with joyful minds and intentions,
they spoke these verses in a single, resonant voice:
The Buddha does not pass into parinirvāṇa, nor does the Dharma perish;
yet, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, he manifests parinirvāṇa.
The Blessed Buddha is inconceivable; the Tathāgata possesses an eternal body, yet he displays various magnificent arrays for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

Then, indeed, the bodhisattva Ruciraketu, having heard from those Blessed Buddhas and from those two holy men the teaching on the lifespan of the Blessed Śākyamuni, was satisfied, uplifted, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer; he became suffused with a sublime joy and rapture.
While this exposition on the measure of the Tathāgata’s lifespan was being taught, immeasurable and incalculable beings conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And those Tathāgatas have now passed away.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Measure of the Tathāgata’s Lifespan," in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the King of Supreme Sūtras.
(Bagchi 10) // The Chapter on the Dream //

Then, indeed, a bodhisattva named Ruciraketu, while asleep and having entered into a dream, saw a golden drum made of gold, shining all around like the orb of the sun; and he saw immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas at the foot of jewel-trees,
seated upon lion-thrones made of lapis lazuli, surrounded by assemblies of many hundreds of thousands.
While they were being honored and preaching the Dharma,
he saw there a man in the form of a brahmin striking that drum;
and there he heard this kind of verse issuing forth from the sound of the drum:
Then, immediately upon awakening, the bodhisattva Ruciraketu recollected those verses of the Dharma teaching.

While recollecting them, at the end of that night, he departed from the great city of Rājagṛha together with many thousands of living beings and approached Gṛdhrakūṭa, the king of mountains, where the Blessed One was staying; having approached, [he went] to the Blessed One.
Having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated him three times, he sat down to one side.

Then, the bodhisattva Ruciraketu, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, spoke those very verses of instruction which he had heard within his dream through the sound of the drum.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Dream," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Glorious Suvarṇaprabhāsottama.
(Bagchi 11) // The Chapter on the Teaching //
For one night, while I was in a state of sleep,
I unweariedly beheld a beautiful drum, possessing a golden radiance on all sides.
Like the blazing sun shining forth in every direction,
the Buddhas were seen everywhere, illuminating the ten directions on all sides.
Seated upon jewel-trees and on radiant lapis lazuli,
they were illuminated by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands.
He saw a drum being beaten by one in the form of a brahmin;
as it was being struck, these verses were heard from it: Suv_4.4 //
By this most excellent drum of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, may the sufferings in the triple-thousand world-system be stilled—
the sufferings of the lower realms, the sufferings of the world of Yama, and likewise the sufferings of poverty in the world.
By this sounding of the drum, may all calamities in the world be pacified;
O Lord of Munis, may all beings everywhere have their hearts struck [by peace], and likewise be free from fear, with their fears stilled.
Just as the Great Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, is endowed with all noble qualities,
so may all living beings become oceans of virtue, possessed of the qualities of the factors of enlightenment and meditative concentration.
By this sounding of the drum’s resonance, may all sentient beings possess the voice of Brahmā;
may they realize the supreme awakening of the noble limbs of Buddhahood and turn the auspicious wheel of Dharma.
May they remain for inconceivable eons and teach the Dharma for the benefit of the world;
may they destroy the afflictions, dispel sufferings, and pacify passion, as well as hatred and delusion. (Suv 4.9)
May those beings who dwell in the realms of misery, their limbs ablaze with fiercely burning fires, hear the sound of the drum proclaiming: "Homage be to the Buddha! and may they obtain these words.
May all beings remember their past lives— through hundreds of births, thousands of births, and tens of millions of births—
and by constantly recollecting the Lord of Munis, may they hear his sublime speech.
By this sound resounding from the drum, may they always obtain union with the Buddhas;
may they indeed avoid evil deeds and practice wholesome and auspicious actions.
May all beings, including humans and asuras, entreat her for the sake of requesting the teaching;
and by this sounding of the drum-like voice, may I fulfill all their [wishes].
Those beings born in the terrible hells, their limbs ablaze with a fiercely burning fire,
wandering about while overcome by grief— they shall find relief through this [teaching].
May all the sufferings of those sentient beings who are most cruel and terrible— whether in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, or in the world of humans—
be pacified by this sounding of the drum.
For those who are without refuge, without protection, and without a sanctuary, may I become their savior, their sanctuary, and their supreme refuge. (Suv_4.16)
May the Buddhas, whose minds are filled with love and compassion, attend to me;
may those established in the ten directions accept my transgression.
Whatever evil karma I have previously committed, however terrible it may be,
I shall confess it all while standing before the One Endowed with the Ten Powers.
Not honoring my mother and father, not recognizing the Buddhas, and not understanding what is wholesome, whatever evil I have committed—[I confess it]. (Suv 4.19)
Whatever evil I have committed while intoxicated by the pride of wealth, by the pride of my noble lineage and physical beauty, and by the intoxication of youth; Suv_4.20 //
Whatever evil I have committed through ill-conceived thoughts, ill-spoken words, or even through misdeeds, failing to perceive their harmful consequences; Suv_4.21.
By wandering with the intellect of a child, with a mind shrouded in ignorance,
under the influence of evil friends, and with a mind agitated by the afflictions.
Whatever evil has been committed by me through attachment to the pleasure of play, under the sway of grief and disease, or due to the fault of insatiable greed for wealth; Suv_4.23 //
Whatever evil has been committed by me through association with ignoble people, due to envy and stinginess, and because of the fault of deceit and poverty; Suv_4.24 //
At this time when calamities have arrived, because of fear regarding sensual desires,
whatever evil has been committed by me even while lacking sovereignty— Suv_4.25.
Whatever evil has been committed by me, whether under the sway of a restless mind or through the power of desire and anger, or even when afflicted by hunger and thirst; Suv_4.26 //
Whatever evil has been committed by me for the sake of drink, for the sake of food, for the sake of clothing, or for the sake of women and wealth, through various afflictions and torments; Suv_4.27.
Whatever evil I have committed through body, speech, and mind, and whatever conduct I have engaged in within the three realms—
all that, in these forms, I now confess.
Whatever disrespect I may have shown toward the Buddhas, the Dharmas, and likewise toward the Śrāvakas— all that I now confess. (Suv 4.29)
Whatever disrespect I may have shown toward Pratyekabuddhas or Bodhisattvas, all of that I now confess.
Whatever true Dharma I may have ever rejected out of ignorance,
and whatever lack of respect I showed toward my mother and father— all that I now confess.
Out of foolishness, out of childishness, being shrouded by pride and arrogance,
and through passion, hatred, and delusion— I confess all of that.
Having worshipped the Jinas, the possessors of the ten powers, throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
I shall deliver all sentient beings from suffering in the ten directions.
I shall establish all inconceivable sentient beings on the ten stages;
for by abiding upon the ten stages, may they all become Tathāgatas.
For the sake of each and every sentient being, I would practice for tens of millions of eons,
doing everything possible to liberate them from the ocean of suffering.
To those beings I would teach this profound teaching called *Suvarṇaprabhottamā*, which brings about the exhaustion of all karma.
Whatever extremely terrible evil has been committed over thousands of eons— by confessing it all at once, may it all go to destruction.
I shall teach this unsurpassed Dharma, the Golden Light;
may those who hear this auspicious teaching attain the complete exhaustion of their evils.
I shall abide on the ten stages within that excellent ocean of the ten jewels, illuminating them with the qualities of a Buddha and ferrying them across the ocean of existence.
And by means of the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha, may I fulfill omniscience— that vast flood of Buddhas, that profound ocean of virtues. (Suv 4.40)
Through hundreds of thousands of samādhis, through inconceivable dhāraṇīs,
and through the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening, may you become the supreme among those possessing the ten powers.
Look upon me, O Buddha, with a mind of compassionate attention;
may you accept my transgression and deliver me from fear.
Whatever evil was committed by me previously throughout hundreds of eons—
for its sake I am sorrowful in mind, wretched, and afflicted by craving.
I am afraid, for I am an evildoer with a perpetually base mind;
wherever I shall wander, there is no auspiciousness anywhere.
May all the compassionate Buddhas, the Victors who remove the fear of sentient beings,
accept my transgression and deliver me from fear.
May the Tathāgatas cause the fruit of my afflictions and karma to flow away;
may the Buddhas bathe me with the stainless waters of compassion.
I confess all evil that was committed by me in the past, and whatever evil I have now; I confess it all.
In the future, having encountered all [consequences] through every evil deed,
I shall not conceal that sin which may have been my own misdeed.
The threefold action of the body, the fourfold action of speech,
and the threefold action of the mind— all that I now confess.
Whatever tenfold karma has been committed through body, speech, and that which was conceived by the mind— all that I now confess.
Having abandoned the ten unwholesome paths and cultivated the ten wholesome ones,
I shall abide on the ten stages and behold the Supreme One of Ten Powers.
"And whatever evil karma of mine brings about undesirable results,
all that I shall confess while standing before the Buddhas. (Suv 4.52)
Whatever wholesome karma is performed here in this Jambudvīpa, and whatever is performed in other world-systems, may I rejoice in all of it.
And whatever merit has been acquired by me through body, speech, and mind—
by that root of virtue may I touch the unsurpassed awakening.
Whatever extremely terrible evil was committed by me, whose childish intellect is trapped in the perilous course of existence,
I now confess all that sin while standing before the presence of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
That accumulated evil, in the peril of birth, in the peril of the proliferation of various desires,
in the peril of the world, in the peril of existence, and in the peril of the afflictions created by all fools.
In the peril of a mind agitated by fickleness and passion, and even in the perils of encountering evil friends;
in the peril of cyclic existence and the peril of attachment, and even in the perils of the darkness of hatred and delusion.
In this time of perilous and inexhaustible distress, and amidst the hardships of failing to acquire merit,
I stand before the peerless Jina and confess all those evils.
I pay homage to the Buddhas, who are like oceans of virtue, golden-hued and illuminating the ends of the quarters;
I go for refuge to those Victors and bow my head to all those Conquerors.
Golden-hued, with a brilliance like the mountain of gold, his body possesses eyes as pure and clear as lapis lazuli;
he is the Buddha-sun, the source of the blazing light of glory, majesty, and fame, whose radiance of compassion dispels the thick darkness of ignorance.
Stainless, most beautiful, with limbs resplendent, his body emerged from the pure gold of the sun that is the Perfectly Awakened One;
like a blazing fire to those whose minds are scorched by the fire of the afflictions, he is the refreshing mass of rays from the moon that is the Sage. (Suv 4.61)
Bearing the thirty-two marks, with graceful senses and limbs, adorned with the secondary characteristics, your body is most beautiful and resplendent;
blazing with the fire of glorious merit and a dense web of rays, you stand like the sun in the three worlds amidst the darkness.

O Great Sage, you shine like the sun, with a vast and variegated complexion as pure as beryl; your body is copper-red, silver, crystal, and crimson, and you radiate a web of rays adorned with many diverse ornaments. Suv_4.63.
In the midst of the flood of calamities that has fallen into the river of saṃsāra— agitated by grief, with death as its water and old age as its waves—
in this ocean of suffering with its most violent and trembling currents, ferry us across with the nets of rays from the sun that is the Sugata!
I pay homage to the Buddhas whose limbs blaze like gold, whose bodies are illuminated by a golden hue;
who are mines of wisdom, the essence of all the three worlds, possessing diverse forms and limbs endowed with auspicious marks.
Just as the water in the ocean is immeasurable, and just as the earth is infinite with its minute particles of dust;
just as Mount Meru is equal to the infinite with its rocks, and just as space is infinite and boundless.
In the same way, the qualities of the Buddha are infinite; indeed, they cannot be known by all sentient beings.
Even if one were to contemplate them for many eons, it would not be possible to know their ultimate extent of qualities. (Suv_4.67)
The earth with its mountains, its peaks, and its oceans, along with all its hosts, might be known even in the course of many eons;
the water, down to the tip of a single hair, might be measured; but the limit of the excellence of a Buddha’s qualities cannot be reached.
May all beings become such as this, endowed with virtue, complexion, and ten millionfold fame;
with bodies beautified by the primary marks and adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics.
By this wholesome karma, may I before long become a Buddha in the world;
may I teach the Dharma for the benefit of the world and liberate beings who are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
May I conquer Māra along with his power and his army; may I set in motion the auspicious Wheel of Dharma;
may I remain for inconceivable eons and satisfy sentient beings with the nectar of immortality from my own hand.
May I fulfill the six unsurpassed perfections just as the previous Victors did in the past;
may I destroy the afflictions, dispel sufferings, and pacify passion, as well as hatred and delusion.
May I always possess the recollection of my past lives throughout hundreds of births, thousands of births, and tens of millions of births;
may I constantly remember the Lord of Munis and hear their sublime speech.
By this wholesome karma, may I always obtain the company of Buddhas;
may I indeed avoid evil deeds and practice meritorious acts that produce purity. (Suv 4.74)
May all the evils of all living beings in all fields throughout the world be pacified;
and may those beings who have impaired faculties or missing limbs now possess all wholesome faculties.
May all those in the ten directions whose limbs are weakened and emaciated by disease, and who have become dependent on others,
be swiftly liberated from illness and regain health, strength, and their sensory faculties.
May all those beings who have encountered hundreds of various calamities, having been seized as victims to be executed by wicked kings and thieves,
and who are suffering from the miseries that have befallen them— may they all be liberated from those hundreds of most terrible fears.
Those who are oppressed, tormented by bonds and fetters, and indeed situated amidst various calamities;
those agitated by many thousands of miseries, and who have encountered diverse, terrifying, and dreadful sorrows.
May they all be released from their bonds; may those who have been beaten be freed from their beatings;
may those condemned to death be spared their lives; and may all who have fallen into calamity become free from fear.
May those beings who are oppressed by hunger and thirst obtain various kinds of food and drink;
may the blind see diverse forms, and may the deaf hear delightful sounds. (Suv 4.80)
May those who are naked obtain variegated garments; may destitute beings obtain wealth;
and may all beings possess abundant money, grain, and various jewels, and be happy.
May no one experience painful sensations; may all beings become endowed with good vision.
May they always possess beautiful, pleasing, and gentle forms, and may they be perpetually filled with manifold happiness.
The citizens of Manaḥśānta possess abundant merit; there are lutes, drums, kettledrums, and sweet-sounding instruments;
and there are springs, lakes, lotus ponds, and reservoirs filled with golden lotuses, blue lotuses, and water-lilies.
By the mere thought of them, may there be food and drink, as well as clothing;
wealth, gold, ornaments of jewels and pearls, and various gems such as gold and lapis lazuli.
May there be no sounds of suffering anywhere in the world, and may not even a single being perceive anything disagreeable;
may they all possess noble complexions and become illuminators for one another.
Whatever prosperity exists in the world of men, may that arise for them through the application of their minds;
may all their intentions be fulfilled by the fruit of merit together with the mere thought [of it]. (Suv_4.86)
May the trees rain down perfumes, garlands, ointments, incense, powders, and full blossoms at the three times of day; may sentient beings receive them and be satisfied.
May they perform inconceivable worship in the ten directions to all the Tathāgatas,
together with the Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas, and to the Dharma that is established in awakening.
May they all avoid low rebirths and cross over by means of the waves and movements of the Eightfold Path;
may they attain the form of the King of Jinas and always enjoy the company of the Buddhas.
May they always be of noble birth, with treasuries overflowing with abundant wealth and grain;
may they be adorned with beauty, valor, glory, and fame for many eons.
May all women always become men, brave, heroic, wise, and learned;
may they all constantly practice for the sake of awakening and practice the six perfections.
May they behold the Buddhas in the ten directions, seated comfortably upon excellent jewel-trees,
resting upon lion-thrones of lapis lazuli, and may they hear the Dharma as it is being proclaimed. (Suv 4.92)
Those evil deeds previously accumulated by me during the perils of existence have been conquered;
may all those who delight in evil deeds be utterly exhausted and rendered indistinguishable from nothingness.

May all those beings dwelling in the bonds of existence, firmly fettered by the snares of saṃsāra, be illuminated by the lamps of wisdom; may they be liberated from their bonds and be freed from all sufferings.
Whatever beings there may be here in Jambudvīpa, and those in other world-systems as well, whatever profound and manifold merit they perform— I rejoice in all that merit.
By this very merit acquired through rejoicing, and through what has been earned by body, speech, and mind, may my fulfillment of the vow be fruitful; may I touch the stainless, unsurpassed awakening.
Whoever always honors and pleases the Ones Possessing the Ten Powers with a mind that is serene, pure, and stainless,
through this confession and dedication, shall avoid the miserable realms for sixty eons.
By means of these verses thus described, men, women, Brahmins, and Kṣatriyas—
whoever shall please the Sage with palms joined in reverence— shall remember their births throughout all hundreds of lifetimes. (Suv_4.98)
With all his limbs and all his faculties adorned, endowed with diverse and perfect qualities,
and always highly honored by kings and lords of men— such as he shall be in various places.
They have not performed wholesome deeds in the presence of even one Buddha,
nor in two, nor in three, nor in five, nor in ten.
Likewise, they have performed wholesome deeds in the presence of thousands of Buddhas,
such that this teaching shall enter into their ears.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsottama.
(Bagchi 24) // The Chapter on the Praise of Kamalākara to All the Tathāgatas //
Then the Blessed One said this to that family deity Bodhisattvasamuccayā:
"Furthermore, O family deity, at that time and on that occasion, there was a king named Suvarṇabhujendra.
With this *Sarvatathāgatastava* (Praise of All Tathāgatas), Kamalākara extolled the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present."

To those Victors who have appeared in the past, those who are now present, and those who abide in the worlds of the ten directions—to all those Victors I prostrate; I shall praise that assembly of Victors.

To the Lord of Munis, peaceful, profoundly tranquil, and pure, whose body is illuminated by a golden radiance; the Buddha whose voice surpasses that of all gods and asuras, possessing the resonance of Brahmā’s speech and the thunderous sound of a great roar.
His hair is like a tree crowned with bees, resembling dark and beautifully curled kāśa grass;
his teeth are as white as a conch shell or snow, and his navel shines, resplendent like gold.
With large, pure, and beautiful blue eyes, shining like the luster of a falling blue lotus;
with a broad and excellent tongue like the gold of a lotus, his lotus-like face possesses the radiance of a lotus.
The Sage’s body has a tuft of hair between the eyebrows like a conch shell or a lotus fiber, with a rightward curl and the color of beryl;
his limbs possess the luster of a black bee, like the subtle moon when it is waning.
(25) His face is elevated with a prominent nose, soft as refined gold; his nose is excellent, distinguished, and straight.
O portion of all the Victors, you are always gentle. Suv_5.6 //
On each single pore-tip of his skin, there is a curl of fine hair turning to the right;
it is dark blue in hue, appearing like a blazing earring, and his beautiful neck is adorned with a crown that shines with a deep blue luster.
His body was born with a radiance equal to that of all the worlds, honored in every direction throughout the world;
he had brought infinite suffering in the three realms to complete peace and satisfied all sentient beings with every form of happiness.
In the realms of hell-beings, in the realms of animals, and in the realms of hungry ghosts, gods, asuras, and humans— among all those beings,
he bestows every happiness, and all the lower realms are completely pacified.
His appearance was like refined gold, silver, and the finest metal; his body was radiant with the luster of molten gold.
His face was as pure as the gentle moon, and his countenance was beautifully bright and spotless, like a blossoming lotus.
With a body as tender as the down of a young fawn, like a lion in its unassailable prowess, with long,
hanging arms, he was like a śāla creeper swayed by the wind.

The Lord of Munis, blazing with the radiance of space and emitting rays of light like a thousand suns scorching all, illuminates the entire infinite realm with his stainless and excellent body. (Suv 5.12)
The entire network of moons, stars, and suns throughout hundreds of thousands of infinite fields—
all these were brought to completion for the sake of the radiant illumination of the Buddha’s light.
May sentient beings behold the sun-like Tathāgata, the lamp illuminating the world, the Buddha-sun who shines throughout hundreds of thousands of infinite fields.
With a body adorned by hundreds of thousands of merits, his limbs decorated with every excellence;
like a majestic lordly elephant, the arm of the Victor has hands adorned with pure and auspicious marks.
Those Buddhas who have passed away are as numerous as the atoms of dust upon the surface of the earth, equal to the number of subtle particles.
Those who are like subtle dust, and those who abide like subtle dust.
With a serene mind, I offer salutations to those Victors with my body, speech, and mind; with the offering of flowers and fragrances, and with hundreds of verses of praise. Suv_5.17.
Even with hundreds of tongues, one could not describe the qualities of the Buddhas in hundreds of thousands of eons;
for those virtues of the Victors that consist in the cessation of evil are supreme, foremost, diverse, and manifold. (Suv 5.18)
The virtues of even a single Jina cannot be fully expressed by anyone, even with hundreds of tongues;
for it would be impossible for all the Jinas together to speak in detail of even a single virtue.

The entire multitude of all the realms of gods, filling even the peak of existence with water, could perhaps be measured by grasping a single hair; but the single quality of the Sugatas cannot be measured at all.
All that has been described and praised by me with a serene body and speech—
by means of the supreme fruit of the merit accumulated by this, may all sentient beings attain the state of a Jina.
Having thus praised the Buddha, the lord of men, the king made this aspiration:
"In whatever place and at whatever time I may be born throughout infinite future eons..."
In such a dream I see a drum like this; there I hear such a teaching.
In such births, O Lotus-Mine of Praise to the Jinas, may I obtain the power of recollection.
The qualities of the Buddha are infinite and incomparable, and even those which are difficult to attain in thousands of eons—
one might hear of them even while dreaming, and one might teach them even while awake during the day. (Suv 5.24)
May I liberate sentient beings from the ocean of suffering and fulfill them with all six perfections;
thereafter, may I attain unsurpassed awakening, and may my buddha-field be beyond compare.
By the ripening fruit of the gift of the drum and for the sake of praising all the Victors, I behold the Lord Śākyamuni face to face; indeed, I shall receive a prophecy there.
May I obtain there, for both these boys, my two sons Kanakendra and Kanakaprabhāsvara, the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
And those beings who are unprotected, without refuge, deprived of shelter, and fallen into despair—
may I become for them all in the future their protection, their ultimate resort, and their refuge.

May I practice for the sake of enlightenment throughout future eons as many as those in the past limit, acting as the creator of the cessation of the arising of suffering and the source of all happiness.
Through the teaching of the supreme *Svarṇaprabhāsa*, may my ocean of evil be dried up;
may my ocean of karma be scattered, and may my ocean of afflictions be severed. (Suv 5.30)
May I fulfill the ocean of merit; may I purify the ocean of wisdom.
By the power of the radiance of stainless wisdom, may I become an ocean of all virtuous qualities.

Filled with the jewels of the qualities of awakening, and by the power of the radiance of the golden voice of teaching, may there be the radiance of merit for me; may the radiance of awakening purify me.
My body shall possess a radiance, a splendor of merit, and a brilliance that shines forth;
may I always be endowed with the power of merit, becoming the most distinguished throughout the entire three worlds.
May I ferry across the ocean of suffering and become like an ocean of all happiness;
may I practice for the sake of awakening throughout future eons, as many as those that have passed since the beginningless past.
Just as the distinguished fields of all the Victors in the three worlds possess infinite qualities,
so shall my own field possess infinite qualities throughout the entirety of the future.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Praise of All Tathāgatas by Kamalākara," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
(Bagchi 30) // The Chapter on Emptiness //
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
In other inconceivable sūtras, the dharmas of emptiness have been taught in great detail;
therefore, in this most excellent of sūtras, these dharmas of emptiness are taught to you in brief.
A being of little intelligence, lacking understanding, is indeed unable to know all phenomena;
behold how, by means of this most excellent king of sutras, the phenomena of emptiness have been taught here in brief.
By means of other skillful methods and principles of reasoning, for the sake of generating compassion within sentient beings,
this supreme king of sutras has been revealed, so that all sentient beings may indeed understand it as it truly is.
And this body is like an empty village, while the sense-faculties are like six villages of thieves;
though they all dwell together in one village, they do not recognize one another.
The eye faculty runs toward forms; the ear faculty [runs] by means of investigating sounds;
the nose faculty is captivated by various fragrances; and the tongue faculty constantly runs toward tastes.
The body-faculty rushes toward touch; the mind-faculty [rushes] through the investigation of phenomena.
Thus, the six faculties each rush toward their own respective objects one after another. (Suv 6.6)
For the mind is like an illusion, flickering and wandering among the objects of the six sense-faculties;
it is like a man running through an empty village, beset by enemies and thieves. (Suv 6.7)
They understand how the mind relies upon the six objects and the range of the sense faculties:
form, sound, as well as smell, taste, touch, and likewise the range of mental phenomena.
And the mind, flickering like a bird, enters into all six sense faculties;
wherever it rests upon a faculty, let that faculty not consider itself to be the knower.
The body is motionless and devoid of activity; it is essence-less, arising from conditions, produced by unreal conceptualization, like a stationary mechanical device—a hollow village. (Suv 6.10)
Just as earth, water, fire, and wind exist in various places within a village infested by thieves,
always mutually opposed to one another, just like venomous serpents in a single house; (Suv 6.11)
Those serpents of the elements are of four kinds: two move upward and two move downward;
whether in pairs or individually, in all directions and intermediate points, those serpents of the elements are destroyed.
The serpent of the earth and the serpent of the waters—these two go downward to their destruction;
the serpent of fire and the serpent of wind—these two indeed move upward to the end of space.
And the mind, abiding within consciousness, having gone according to karma performed in the past,
proceeds among gods and humans and in the three lower realms, as it was enacted in previous existences.
The body, having reached the end of the depletion of phlegm, wind, and bile, is filled with excrement, urine, and impurities;
devoid of beauty, it is filled with tiny worms and, when cast into the cemetery, becomes like a piece of wood.
Behold, O deity, how many beings or persons there are here in this way;
for all these phenomena are indeed empty, arising from ignorance and through conditions. (Suv 6.16)
All these great elements are non-existent because they lack the intrinsic nature of great elements;
therefore, these elements are indeed unarisen, non-existent, and are never found to exist at any time.
Because they arise from conditions, ignorance is indeed non-existent; yet it is called "ignorance.
Therefore, I have said: this ignorance consists of formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth.
The six sense bases, contact, and likewise feeling, craving, grasping, and becoming;
birth, old age, death, grief, and calamities—these sufferings of conditioned phenomena are inconceivable.

Just as things exist within the wheel of saṃsāra—those that have arisen from what was unreal, those that have not arisen, and those that are impossible—you shall yourselves sever the course of views and the improper mental deliberations [regarding them]. (Suv 6.20)
Cut through the web of afflictions with the sword of wisdom; behold the abode of the aggregates as empty.
Touch that sublime quality of awakening, and open for me the door to the city of immortality.

He beheld that vessel of the city of immortality; having entered that auspicious abode of the city of immortality, he will satisfy himself with the essence of nectar. The excellent drum of the Dharma has been struck by me. (Suv_6.22)
The conch of the excellent Dharma has been filled by me; the torch of the excellent Dharma has been kindled by me;
the rain of the excellent Dharma has been well-showered by me; and the enemies that are the afflictions of others have been defeated by me.
I have raised high the supreme banner of the Dharma; I have ferried across the oceans of sentient beings in existence;
I have closed the three paths to the lower realms, having extinguished for living beings the burning fire of the afflictions.
For in the past, throughout many inconceivable eons, I have indeed honored the Leaders;
having practiced for the sake of awakening with firm vows, I was seeking the body of the True Dharma.

Having renounced both hands and feet, wealth, gold, and ornaments of gems and pearls; having given up his eyes, his head, his beloved wife and sons, and various precious jewels such as gold and beryl—
Having cut down all the trees and forest plants within the triple-thousandfold world system,
and having pulverized them all, one would reduce that to the likeness of fine dust.
Having made a heap of powder reaching as far as the realm of space,
they were unable to divide it even by a fraction, though it was equal to the dust of the earth.
(35) Indeed, all the many sentient beings, as well as those possessed of knowledge— all of them might be counted, but they cannot measure the knowledge of the Jina. Suv_6.29 //
But as for the knowledge of the Great Sage that arises in a single moment,
it could never be calculated even over many millions of eons.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Emptiness," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsottama.
(Bagchi 36) // The Chapter on the Four Great Kings //

Then indeed, the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Great King Virūḍhaka, and the Great King Virūpākṣa rose from their seats, draped their robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Lord, this Sovereign King of Sutras, the Suvarṇaprabhāsottama, has been spoken by all the Tathāgatas, beheld by all the Tathāgatas, endowed with the power of all the Tathāgatas, honored by the assembly of all Bodhisattvas, worshipped by the assembly of all the gods, and brings great joy to the assembly of all the lords of the gods."

He is praised, lauded, extolled, and glorified by all the world-protectors; he illuminates the abodes of all the gods; he bestows supreme happiness upon all sentient beings; he purifies the sufferings of all the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama; he pacifies all fears; he turns back all hostile armies; he quells the wilderness of famine and destroys the wilderness of disease; and he is the illuminator of primordial wisdom.
It brings about supreme peace, calms grief and exhaustion, and pacifies various and manifold calamities, destroying hundreds of thousands of afflictions.
Venerable Blessed One, as this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the king of all sūtras, is being proclaimed in detail to the assembly, our four great kings, together with our armies and retinues,
shall increase through this hearing of the Dharma, through the nectar-like essence of the Dharma, and through the great majesty of our divine bodies.
Vigor, strength, and power will be generated within our bodies;
brilliance, glory, and fortune will enter our bodies.

O Blessed One, we four Great Kings are righteous, speakers of the Dharma, and kings of the Dharma. By means of the Dharma, O Venerable Blessed One, we [shall govern] the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, humans, and mahoragas.
"We shall exercise sovereignty.
O Blessed One, we four Great Kings, together with the twenty-eight yakṣa generals and many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas," [shall do so].
"Constantly and continuously, we shall survey the whole of Jambudvīpa with our divine, pure vision that transcends that of humans;
we shall protect it and bring it to maturity.
For that reason, O Venerable Blessed One, the designation 'World-Protector' has arisen for us four Great Kings."

"O Venerable Blessed One, whatever perversions there may be in this Jambudvīpa, or those who will be afflicted by foreign armies, or those who will be afflicted by famine, or by hundreds of various calamities, thousands of calamities, and hundreds of thousands of calamities,"
"Venerable Blessed One, we four Great Kings shall provide an exhortation for this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtrendrarāja* and for those monks who uphold these king of sutras.

And when, Venerable Blessed One, these Dharma-preaching monks, through our four Great Kings' exhortation and by the empowerment of the Buddha, enter into various regions, in those regions they shall [recite] this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtrendrarāja*."
They shall reveal it in detail;
they shall pacify these various hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of calamities occurring within the sensory realms that are of such a nature.
And, O Venerable Blessed One, in whatever human king’s realm those monks who are preachers of the Dharma and holders of this king of sutras shall appear,

and if that human king should hear this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the king of kings of sutras, and having heard it, should provide protection, rescue, shelter, and guardianship for those monks who are holders of this king of sutras against all adversaries.
"Venerable Blessed One, we four great kings shall provide protection, rescue, assistance, and guardianship for that human king and for all beings within his realm;
we shall provide peace and well-being.
And when, Venerable Blessed One, every human king provides comfort through all necessary articles of well-being for the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who uphold this king of sutras,"

"Venerable Blessed One, we four Great Kings shall treat that king of men with greater honor than all other kings; we shall treat him with reverence, respect, and worship, and we shall cause him to be praised throughout all his realms.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the four Great Kings, saying, "Excellent!"
Excellent, excellent, O Great Kings! Excellent, excellent, O Great Kings!
For you have performed services under previous Victors, planted roots of merit, and attended upon many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
You are righteous and speakers of the Dharma, and you exercise the sovereignty over gods and humans in accordance with the Dharma.

Just as you, O Four Great Kings, have for a long time in the past possessed hearts intent on the welfare of all sentient beings and hearts of loving-kindness for their happiness; as you have been established in the resolute intention for the benefit and happiness of all beings, acting to prevent all that is harmful and being devoted to bringing about every kind of welfare for all sentient beings— so too, you four great kings [should protect] that human king and this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the king of sovereign sūtras.
They will provide protection, rescue, guardianship, and defense for those engaged in worship and honor; they will provide peace and well-being.

By this, O Four Great Kings, together with your armies and retinues and many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, the guidance of the Dharma of the past, future, and present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will be guarded, protected, and upheld by you.
Therefore, for you four Great Kings, together with your armies and retinues, and for many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, there will be victory in the battle between the gods and the asuras,
and the complete defeat of the asuras. This is for the sake of those who uphold this king of sutras, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which crushes all hostile armies.
They will provide protection for the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; they will provide rescue, acceptance, guardianship, peace, and well-being.

Then the great king Vaiśravaṇa, the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the great king Virūḍhaka, and the great king Virūpākṣa rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable Blessed One,

in the future time, in whatever villages, towns, market-towns, districts, kingdoms, or royal capitals this Sovereign King of Sutras, the Suvarṇaprabhāsottama, shall circulate, and in whichever realm of whichever human king it shall arrive—
“Venerable Blessed One, might there be some king of men who, by means of this *Rājaśāstra* of the Devendra-samaya, should exercise kingship;

and while being a listener to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras, he would honor, revere, respect, and worship those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who uphold this king of sūtras, and would constantly and continuously listen to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras?”

By this hearing of the Dharma, may these divine bodies of us four Great Kings together with our entire retinues, as well as of many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas and rākṣasas— who consist of the merit of the nectar of the Dharma that inspires—
be increased by great vital energy; and may great vigor, stamina, strength, splendor, glory, and fortune be increased within our bodies.

Therefore, O Venerable Blessed One, we four Great Kings, together with our armies and retinues and many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas whose bodies and forms are invisible, shall now and in the future go to those villages, cities, towns, districts, kingdoms,
and royal capitals where this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of the best of sūtras, shall circulate.
And for those human kings who listen to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of sutras, we shall provide protection for them and for their parents;
we shall provide rescue, preservation, exemption from punishment, exemption from weapons, and peace and well-being.
We shall also provide protection for those royal families, those kingdoms, and those territories.
We shall provide protection, support, and guardianship; we shall ensure the avoidance of punishment and the avoidance of weapons, and we shall perform rites for peace and well-being.
We shall liberate those territories from all fears, calamities, and afflictions, and we shall turn back the armies of enemy forces.
Should there be any neighboring rival king who is an adversary to that human king who hears, honors, and worships this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the sovereign king of sutras—
And when, Venerable Blessed One, that neighboring rival king has formed such a thought as this:
"I shall approach his realm together with a fourfold army in order to destroy it"—
at that very time and on that occasion, Venerable Blessed One, regarding this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*...
By the power and majesty of this sovereign king of sūtras, that neighboring rival king will engage in battle with other kings; furthermore,
there will be the destruction of his own territory and its inhabitants.
And terrible disturbances caused by kings will arise; planetary afflictions and diseases will manifest within the realm;
and hundreds of various distractions will appear within the realm.
And when, Venerable Blessed One, hundreds of various calamities and hundreds of various disturbances should arise within the territory of that neighboring rival king;
and when, Venerable Blessed One, that neighboring rival king, having mobilized a fourfold army, should depart from his own realm to march against the enemy host;
and wherever this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of the sovereign sūtras, may be, that rival king, together with his fourfold military force, should desire to invade that territory.
"May he wish to destroy it.

O Venerable Blessed One, we four Great Kings, together with our armies and retinues and many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas and rākṣasas whose bodies are invisible, will approach that hostile army as it has set out upon its path."
In that very way, we shall cause them to retreat, we shall bring forth hundreds of various distractions, and we shall create obstacles,
so that that hostile army will not be able to advance into that territory;
how much less, then, could it bring about its destruction?
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to those four great kings, saying:

"Excellent, excellent, O great kings! It is indeed excellent of you, great kings, that for the sake of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—which has been fully accomplished over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons—you have acted thus."
You shall provide protection for those human kings and for the listeners of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of sutras;
you shall provide rescue, acceptance, preservation, peace, and well-being;
and you shall protect those royal families, those cities, those kingdoms, and those territories.
"You shall provide protection, guardianship, and preservation; you shall grant immunity from punishment and immunity from weapons; you shall perform rites for peace and well-being.
You shall liberate those territories from all calamities, misfortunes, states of woe, and afflictions, and you shall turn back the armies of enemy forces."
And you should ensure that this human king throughout all of Jambudvīpa is free from strife, quarreling, contention, and dispute, and that he is devoid of any zeal for conflict;

and so that those four great kings, together with their armies and retinues, may find delight in this Jambudvīpa, in those four thousand cities, in those eighty-four thousand cities, and in each of those respective provinces.
And they would not take delight in royal power and sovereignty, nor would they harm one another because of that mass of wealth;
they would not cause mutual injury.
And each would obtain their kingship according to the accumulation of their own past karma.
They would be content with their own royal sovereignty and would not destroy one another; they would not exert themselves for the sake of destroying others by means of poison.

And just as in this Jambudvīpa, among those eighty-four thousand regional cities, those eighty-four thousand kings— possessing hearts of mutual benefit, hearts of loving-kindness, and hearts of happiness— delight in their respective realms without mutual strife, quarreling, conflict, or dispute; by that merit, [this] belongs to the four Great Kings together with their armies and retinues.
And Jambudvīpa will become prosperous;
it will be well-supplied with food, delightful, crowded with many people, flourishing, and possessed of superior vitality.
Furthermore, all the seasons, months, fortnights, and years will proceed in perfect regularity.
Day and night, the planets, constellations, moon, and sun will move in harmony;
rain will fall upon the earth in due season;
and all sentient beings throughout the entire continent of Jambudvīpa will become prosperous with all kinds of wealth and grain.
They will possess great wealth and be free from stinginess;
they will be generous and endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action,
and for the most part, they will be reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.
And the divine realms will become filled with gods and sons of gods.

(Bagchi 41) Should there be any great king who hears this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the sovereign king of sūtras, and honors and worships it, as well as those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who uphold this sovereign king of sūtras, he shall [arouse] zeal for them.
One should honor, revere, esteem,

and worship [this sutra] for the sake of compassion toward you four great kings, together with your armies and retinues, and toward the many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, while constantly and perpetually listening to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of the best of sūtras.
With this water of the nectar of hearing the Dharma, may he satiate these bodies of yours;
with great vital energy, may he cause these bodies of yours to flourish;
and may he generate in you great vigor, stamina, strength, and physical splendor.
May splendor, glory, and fortune increase for you!
By that act, that king of men will have performed an inconceivable, great, vast, and extensive worship of me, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

By that king of men, an inconceivable, great, and extensive worship with all necessary requisites will have been performed for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of past, future, and present Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
An offering will have been made;
thereby a great protection will have been established for that king of men.
And by that, protection, rescue, guardianship, and preservation for that king will be provided, along with immunity from punishment, immunity from weapons, and peace and well-being.
Great protection will be established for the chief queen, the princes, the entire harem, and the whole royal family;
there will be rescue, acceptance, preservation, peace, and well-being.
Furthermore, all the deities residing in the royal palace will become more vigorous in their vital energy, endowed with happiness and gladness of mind, and they will experience delight.

And those kingdoms and those territories will be well-protected; they will be brought to maturity, free from oppression, and devoid of thorns; all foreign armies will be crushed, and they will be free from calamities and free from afflictions.
When this had been said, the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Great King Virūḍhaka, and the Great King Virūpākṣa—all of them said this to the Blessed One:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, that king of men should have his body well-washed, wear fragrant perfumes, be clothed in new, beautiful garments, and be adorned with various ornaments;
he should also prepare for himself a very low seat."
Having sat upon that seat, one should not be intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty;
nor should the king himself appoint [the throne] too high.
With a mind free from deceit, conceit, intoxication, and arrogance, this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of the sovereign sūtras, should be heard.
And one should conceive the perception of the Teacher toward that Dharma-preaching monk.
At that time, at that moment, that king of men should regard his chief queen, his sons, his daughters, and the entire retinue of the harem with affection and kindness.
The chief queen, the princes, the princesses, and all the members of the harem should be addressed with pleasant words.
Various and manifold offerings for hearing the Dharma should be ordered.
One should satisfy oneself with inconceivable and incomparable joy.
One should gladden [others] with inconceivable joy and happiness;
one should possess the faculty of pleasure;
and one should possess great power for oneself.
One should gladden oneself with great joy;
one should rise up to greet the Dharma-preacher with great affection born of love.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those four Great Kings:
"Furthermore, O Great Kings, at that time and on that occasion, that king of men should don all-white, pale garments of fresh luster;
he should adorn himself with various ornaments and decorations."

With great royal majesty and a grand royal procession, accompanied by various wonderful jewels and auspicious objects, you must depart from that royal palace and go forth to meet that Dharma-preaching monk. And why is that?

For as many steps as the human king traverses there, for that many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons he will turn his back upon saṃsāra; he will become the possessor of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lineages of universal monarchs (cakravartin). And for as many steps as he strides there, by that much he will increase in great, inconceivable royal sovereignty pertaining to the present life.
He will obtain celestial palaces made of the seven precious gems, which are magnificent and sublime, and have endured for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
He will also obtain many hundreds of thousands of divine and noble sons of royal families among humans.
And in all his births, he will attain great sovereignty.
He will be long-lived and live for a long time;
he will possess eloquence, his words will be authoritative, and he will be renowned and possessed of very extensive fame.
He will be happy in the world including its gods, humans, and asuras;
he will obtain sublime and most excellent divine and human pleasures;

and he will possess great strength, bearing the power and speed of a great wrestler, being handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion and lotus-like purity.
In all births, he will encounter the Tathāgata;
he will obtain all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra);
and he will be sustained by an immeasurable mass of merit.
Seeing such qualities and benefits as these, O Great King, that king should rise from his seat for a distance of one yojana to welcome the Dharma-preacher.
He should conceive the perception of the Teacher toward that Dharma-preacher and should generate such a thought.
Today the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will enter this royal palace.

Today the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will instruct his own kinsmen here in the royal palace. I shall hear the teaching of the Dharma, which is something that the whole world finds difficult to believe.
"Today, by hearing this Dharma, I shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Today, I shall have propitiated hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas.
Today, I shall have performed an inconceivable, great, vast, and extensive worship for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present."
Today, my sufferings in the realms of hell, the animal womb, and the world of Yama will be utterly severed.

Today, I shall plant the seeds of roots of merit for the attainment of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of self-existences as Brahmā, Indra, and kings. Today, I shall plant the roots of merit for the attainment of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of self-existences as Śakra.
Today, I shall have planted the seeds of roots of merit for the attainment of the physical forms of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of universal monarchs.

Today, I shall have liberated hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings from saṃsāra. Today, I shall have grasped an inconceivable, most vast, extensive, and boundless mass of merit.
Today, great protection will have been established for me and my entire harem;
today, inconceivable, peerless, unsurpassed, and great peace and well-being will have been established within my royal palace;
and today, this entire realm of mine will be protected.
It will be well-protected, free from oppression, free from anxiety, unsubdued by any foreign armies, and free from calamities and distress.

And when, O Great Kings, that king of men, out of such reverence for the True Dharma, honors, reveres, and respects the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who uphold this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the sovereign king of sutras— then, O Great Kings, it shall be likewise for you four great kings with your armies and retinues, and for those hosts of gods and many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas.

He should grant a direct perception of the factors of the Dharma, by which that king of men, through that very accumulation of merit and accumulation of wholesome roots, as well as through his own person, will increase his great sovereignty of kingship in this present life in an inconceivable way;
he will become endowed with great royal splendor in this present life in an inconceivable way.
He will be adorned with glory, splendor, and majesty;
and all adversaries and all enemies will be thoroughly subdued by means of the Dharma.
When this had been said, the four great kings spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, whatever human king there may be who, with such reverence for the Dharma, should listen to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the sovereign king of sūtras."
One should honor, revere, respect, and worship those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who uphold this king of sutras.
For the sake of us four great kings, one should thoroughly clean that royal palace and sprinkle it with various kinds of scented water.

And we, together with the four great kings, shall listen to that hearing of the Dharma in common for our own sake; and may all the deities witness even a small portion of the merit for the Venerable Blessed One who is seated upon his Dharma-seat, as that king of men burns various incenses for the sake of us four great kings.
"Venerable Blessed One, when these various perfumes are incensed for the sake of worshiping that *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of sutras, various fragrant incense-vines will emerge from them.

At that very instant, moment, and second, above us in the sky within our respective palaces, canopies formed by those various fragrant incense-vines will be established, and we, the four great kings, shall smell sublime fragrances."
And radiances consisting of golden color will appear;
by that radiance, our dwellings will be illuminated.
[This shall be so] for Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, the Great Goddess Sarasvatī, and Dṛḍhā.

Of the Great Goddess Śrī, of the Great Goddess Saṃjayā, of the great yakṣa general Aṣṭāviṃśati, of the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals, of the divine son Maheśvara, of the great yakṣa general Vajrapāṇi,
of the great yakṣa general Māṇibhadra, of Hārītī with her retinue of five hundred sons, and of the nāga king Anavatapta.
And for these, O Venerable Blessed One, while they remain in their respective abodes,
in that very instant, moment, and second, canopies of various fragrant incense-vines shall be established in the sky above,
and they shall smell sublime and diverse fragrances.
And illuminations consisting of golden color will appear;
by that illumination, all the palaces will be illuminated.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the four great kings:

"It is not only above you, the four great kings, while you are each in your own respective abodes, that canopies of various fragrant incense-vines will be established in the atmosphere. For what reason?"

Simultaneously with the burning of various incenses by that king of men for the sake of worship and service of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the sovereign king of sūtras, there shall emerge from his hand, which holds the incense burner, various fragrant incense-vines.
In that very instant, moment, and second, throughout this entire triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, where there are hundreds of millions of moons—
There are one hundred koṭis of Sumerus, kings of mountains; one hundred koṭis of Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountain kings;
one hundred koṭis of the four great continents; one hundred koṭis of the gods of the Four Great Kings; one hundred koṭis of the Trāyastriṃśa gods;
and so on, up to one hundred koṭis of the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
And throughout all those hundreds of millions of trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems, in the realms of the Trāyastriṃśa gods,

canopies of various fragrant incense-vines will be established in the sky above all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, both those residing in their palaces and those moving through the atmosphere.
They shall smell noble and various fragrances,
and illuminations consisting of golden color shall appear;
by those illuminations, all the palaces shall be made radiant.
Jeweled parasols will appear;
they shall smell most sublime and magnificent fragrances, and golden-colored radiances will manifest in all the abodes of the gods. By that radiance, all the abodes of the gods will be illuminated.
Just as in the great trichiliocosm all the celestial palaces of the gods will be suspended in the sky above as parasols made of various fragrant incense-vines,
so too, O Great Kings, by the power of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of supreme sūtras,
various fragrances shall be wafted by the wind from the incense-burner held in the hand of that human king for the sake of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of supreme sūtras.
For the purpose of worship, canopies of various fragrant incense-creepers will be established.
In that very instant, moment, and second, throughout the ten directions, in many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges,

those canopies of various fragrant incense-creepers will be established in the sky above many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas, equal in number to the sands of the river Ganges.

In those Buddha-fields, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they shall smell most sublime and various fragrances and incenses from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
Radiant lights of golden color shall appear, and by that radiance,
those many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shall be illuminated.
