the padma, kumuda, utpala, and likewise the puṇḍarīka.
The sky becomes auspicious, freed from the net of smoke;
the directions become radiant, liberated from darkness and dust.
The sun, with its thousand rays and a web of beams, exceedingly radiant, will, being gladdened by its profound illumination, urge [the world] forward. (Suv 15.67)
Situated within a celestial palace made of Jambūnada gold,
the sons of the gods, Sūrya and Indradeva, are well-satisfied by this discourse.
These lords of sūtras, filled with great joy, arrive in Jambudvīpa;
O, they shall illuminate everywhere with an uninterrupted web of light rays.
As soon as they are awakened, by the stimulation of the network of light rays,
they shall awaken the lotuses covered by various lotus ponds.
Throughout this entire Jambudvīpa, they perfectly ripen the various grains, fruits, and medicinal herbs, and they warm that great earth with their heat.
In that interval, the moon and sun shine with particular brilliance;
the constellations move correctly, and likewise do the winds and rains.
All of Jambudvīpa will everywhere enjoy abundance,
and that kingdom especially where this sūtra exists.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Refuge of Yakṣas," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsottama.
(Bagchi 90) // The Chapter on the Prophecy for Ten Thousand Sons of Gods //
When this had been said, the family deity Bodhisattvasamuccayā addressed the Blessed One:

"By what cause, by what reason, and by what kind of blazing vigor and roots of merit, through the performance and accumulation of which, do these ten thousand sons of the gods, headed by the god Jvalanāntaratejorāja, [now...]"
Having come from the celestial realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, they approach the presence of the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Having heard the prophecy of bodhisattvahood for these three noble beings, they resolve their minds upon awakening (*bodhicitta*).
Just as this noble being Ruciraketu, after many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons have passed in a future time beyond counting—
In the world-system Suvarṇaprabhāsita, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

he will appear in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suvarṇaratnākaracchatrakūṭa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

When that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Suvarṇaratnākaracchatrakūṭa had passed into parinirvāṇa, and when the True Dharma had completely disappeared— in every way, entirely, and in all respects— such that his teaching had vanished,
this boy named Rūpyaketu [appeared].

In the retinue of that Tathāgata, in that very world-system Virajadhvaja, there shall appear in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suvarṇajambudhvajakāñcanābha. When that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Suvarṇadhvajakāñcanāvabhāsa has passed into parinirvāṇa, and when his teaching has entirely and in every way completely disappeared, this boy Rūpyaprabha [shall appear].

Following that Tathāgata, he will attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment right there in that same world-system, Virajadhvaja. He will appear in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suvarṇaśataraśmiprabhāsagarbha—
one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, and a teacher of gods and humans.
And for human beings, there is the Buddha, the Blessed One.
All of them have now been prophesied by the Blessed One to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, O Venerable Blessed One, the extent of the bodhisattva conduct of these ten thousand sons of gods, headed by Jvalanāntaratejorāja, was never before known;
it was not heard that they had previously practiced the six perfections,
nor was it ever heard that they had previously renounced their eyes, feet, heads, dear sons, wives, and daughters.
It is not heard that he has ever previously relinquished wealth, grain, silver, gold, jewels, pearls, diamonds, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, native gold, silver, emeralds, or gems;
nor is it heard that he has ever previously relinquished various kinds of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, beds, seats, palaces, celestial mansions, groves, lotus ponds, or lakes.
It is not heard that they have previously abandoned various elephants, horses, mares, male servants, or female servants; rather,

just as those many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas will, in the past hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons, perform worship with hundreds of thousands of various inconceivable and diverse offerings and all necessary requisites for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable Tathāgatas.
They will renounce the relinquishing of all jewels; they will perform the relinquishing of hands, feet, eyes, head, dear sons, wives, and daughters;
they relinquish the relinquishing of wealth, grain, silver, gold, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and refined gold.

They will relinquish food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, houses, celestial palaces, groves, gardens, lotus ponds, elephants, cattle, horses, mares, female slaves, male slaves, and all their possessions.
Gradually, they will fulfill the six perfections;
having gradually fulfilled the six perfections, they will experience many hundreds of thousands of joys.
Until they receive a prophecy from the Blessed Buddhas under the name of Tathāgata.

"By what cause, by what reason, and by what kind of planted roots of merit, O Venerable Blessed One, do those ten thousand sons of gods, headed by Jvalanāntarajoti-rāja, approach the presence of the Blessed One here to hear the Dharma?
They have now been prophesied by the Blessed One for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
That is to say, after many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons have passed in the future,

they will successively attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in that very world-system called Śālendradhvajāgravatī, belonging to a single family lineage and bearing a single name. Under the name Prasannavadanotpalagandhakūṭa, ten thousand Buddhas will appear in the world throughout the ten directions.
They are Buddhas, Blessed Ones— endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugatas, knowers of the world, unsurpassed leaders of persons to be tamed, teachers of gods and humans.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to that family deity Bodhisattvasamuccayā:
"O family deity, there is a cause; there is a reason for it.
There is that planted root of merit, by the performance and accumulation of which these [deities], headed by Jvalanāntaratejorāja, [have come to be]."
Ten thousand sons of gods currently approach from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven here to hear the Dharma.

O family deity, upon hearing this prophecy of enlightenment for these three holy men, and simultaneously with that hearing, they shall attain a sense of wonder, joy, and serene faith toward this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras.
To that extent, they become endowed with a perfectly pure mind resembling stainless lapis lazuli;
they become endowed with a profound clarity of mind resembling the stainless, vast, and expansive expanse of space;
and they have grasped an immeasurable mass of merit, beginning with those headed by Jvalanāntaratejorāja, who are the deities of the caityas.
Upon hearing this sovereign king of sūtras, ten thousand sons of gods attained a state of wonder and serene faith;
they became endowed with such a perfectly pure mind, resembling stainless beryl, until they reached the stage of receiving the prophecy.

O noble goddess, by this accumulation of roots of merit from hearing the Dharma, and through the power of their former vows, these ten thousand sons of gods, headed by Jvalanāntaratejorāja, have now [attained] unsurpassed...
They have been prophesied for perfect enlightenment.
And what, O Kuladevatā, are those former vows?
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Prophecy of the Ten Thousand Sons of the Gods," in the *Śrī-Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtrendrarāja*.
(Bagchi 93) // The Chapter on the Allaying of Diseases //
In the past, O tutelary deity, at a time more immeasurable, vast, inconceivable, and incalculable than countless aeons ago, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Ratnaśikhin—
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and [men].
And for humans, there was the Buddha, the Blessed One. Furthermore, O family deity, at that time and on that occasion, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaśikhin— the Blessed One—
had passed into parinirvāṇa, and when the true Dharma had disappeared and the semblance of the true Dharma (saddharmapratirūpaka) was prevailing;
There was a king named Sureśvaraprabha,
righteous and a king of Dharma, who protected his kingdom through Dharma and not through unrighteousness, acting like a mother and father to all beings dwelling within his realm.
Furthermore, O family deity, at that time and in that period, in the realm of King Sureśvaraprabha, there was a merchant named Jaṭindhara.
There was a physician, a healer, who was highly skilled in the primary constituents of the body and fully accomplished in the eightfold science of medicine.
Indeed, O Kuladevatā, at that time and on that occasion, a son named Jalavāhana was born to that merchant Jaṭindhara;

he was handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold, endowed with the most excellent complexion and lotus-like beauty, skilled in various treatises, having mastered the course of all sciences, proficient in scripts, numerals, and calculation, and an expert in all arts.
It came to pass, O family deity, that at that time and on that occasion, within the realm of King Sureśvaraprabha, many hundreds of thousands of beings were afflicted by various diseases;
tormented by manifold ailments, they experienced sensations that were painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable.

Furthermore, O family deity, at that time and on that occasion, a mind of supreme compassion arose in the merchant’s son Jalavāhana for the sake of those many hundreds of thousands of beings who were afflicted by various diseases and oppressed by various ailments.

These many hundreds of thousands of beings, afflicted by various diseases and tormented by various ailments, are now experiencing sensations that are painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable.
And this father of mine, Jaṭiṃdhara, the guild-leader and physician, is supremely skilled in the elements and endowed with the eightfold science of Ayurveda; yet he is old and decrepit.
An old man, advanced in years, having reached the end of his life’s journey, his body aged and trembling, leaning upon a staff, approached every village, town, market-town, kingdom, and capital.

Seeing these many hundreds of thousands of beings afflicted by various diseases and oppressed by various ailments, he thought: "I must now approach this very father, Jaṭindhara, and inquire about superior skill in order to liberate them from their various maladies."
"By means of that skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*) which I have been asked about, I shall go everywhere—to villages, towns, market-towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
Having gone there, I shall liberate those many hundreds of thousands of beings who are touched by various diseases and oppressed by various ailments from their various maladies.
Then, O noble goddess, at that time and on that occasion, Jalavāhana, the son of the guild-leader, approached his father, Jaṭiṃdhara, the guild-leader.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of his father Jaṭindhara, he stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
Standing to one side, Jalavāhana, the son of the guild-president, questioned his father, the guild-president Jaṭindhara, regarding his skill in the elements with these verses:
Those sense faculties are observed to change as the elements undergo transformation;
by what time do the diseases of embodied beings arise? (Suv 17.1)
And how should one eat food at the proper times so that it brings happiness,
and by which means the internal body is not harmed by the bodily fire?
How should medical treatment be administered for wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman), as well as when a combination of all three (saṃnipāta) has arisen? How may the disease be pacified?
At what time does the wind become disturbed, and when does the bile become disturbed?
At what time does the phlegm become disturbed, by which human beings are afflicted?
Then, indeed, the merchant Jaṭīṃdhara, having understood the son of the merchant Jalavāhana’s skill regarding the elements through these verses, taught it to him.
In this context, the rainy season is known to consist of three months, as is the autumn;
likewise, the winter consists of three months, and the summer likewise consists of three.
Thus is the sequence of months; six seasons are known as a year consisting of twelve months.
Food and drink are likewise digested by physicians who have demonstrated their skill through their knowledge. (Suv 17.6)
Moreover, within the course of a year, the elements of the sense faculties also undergo transformation;
and as these sense faculties transform, various diseases arise for embodied beings.

In that very context, the physician’s fourfold [expertise] regarding the six seasons within the interval of three months—consisting of skill in the six elements and knowledge of food and medicine respectively—should be understood. (Suv 17.8)
Disturbances dominated by wind arise in the rainy season; there is an aggravation of the humors in autumn when the sky is clear;
likewise, in the winter season, there is a combination of all three humors, and those dominated by phlegm occur in the summer.
In the rainy season, one should consume substances with unctuous, hot, salty, and sour tastes; in the autumn, those that are unctuous, sweet, and cold;
in the winter, those that are sweet, sour, and unctuous; and in the summer, those that are dry, hot, and pungent.
One with a predominance of phlegm becomes aggravated immediately after eating; one with a predominance of bile becomes aggravated while the food is being digested;
and one with a predominance of wind becomes aggravated once digestion is complete—such is the provocation of the three humors.

It performs a strengthening treatment for one who is emaciated, acts as a purgative, increases bile, and is endowed with the three qualities; likewise, it brings relief in cases of the combined humors (*saṃnipāta*) and alleviates phlegm during the onset of paroxysms. (Suv 17.12)
One should recognize that in a *sannipāta* [disorder] involving *pitta*, there is an excess of *vāta*; in the joints (*parva*), there is an excess of *kapha*.
Whatever the time, whatever the constituent element (*dhātu*), and whatever the locus may be, food, drink, and medicine appropriate for that must be administered. (Suv 17.13)

Then indeed, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana, having been questioned by that prognosticator regarding such expertise in the elements (*dhātu-kausalya*), attained mastery over the entire eightfold science of medicine (*aṣṭāṅga-āyurveda*).

Furthermore, O family deity, at that time and on that occasion, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana, having traveled throughout all the villages, towns, market towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals within the domain of King Sureśvaraprabha, [proceeded].
He thus comforted all those many hundreds of thousands of beings who were afflicted by various diseases and tormented by various ailments:
"Do not fear! I am a physician; I am a physician," he declared of himself, "I shall liberate you from your various diseases.
O goddess of the family, as soon as they heard these words being spoken by the merchant’s son Jalavāhana, all those many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings—
They became filled with great joy;
they attained consolation and were endowed with inconceivable gladness and mental well-being.
At that time, at that moment, by means of that joy, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings [were likewise affected].
Those touched by various diseases and oppressed by various ailments were liberated from those various diseases; they became free from illness and devoid of sickness.
They came to be endowed with their former strength, power, and vigor.

Furthermore, O family deity, at that time and on that occasion, for those many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings who were touched by various diseases and oppressed by various ailments...
Whosoever were afflicted by more severe conditions,

they all approached Jalavāhana, the son of the merchant; and having approached him, he prescribed various medicinal preparations for those hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings who were touched by various diseases and oppressed by various ailments.

In all those royal capitals, all those many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings who were afflicted by various diseases and tormented by various ailments were liberated from their various maladies by Jalavāhana, the son of the merchant.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Diseases," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
(Bagchi 98) // The Chapter on the Taming of the Fish by Jalavāhana //

Furthermore, O goddess of the family, within the realm of King Sureśvaraprabha, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana rendered all sentient beings free from disease; with their afflictions diminished and their former vigor, strength, and physical health restored, they all delighted in the joy of enthusiasm and played.
They provided entertainment,
they gave gifts,
and they performed meritorious deeds.

The merchant’s son Jalavāhana, a healer of diseases through the happiness of great medical gifts, must certainly become a Bodhisattva through direct perception. He had mastered the entire eightfold science of medicine (*aṣṭāṅgāyurvaidya*).
Furthermore, that merchant’s son Jalavāhana had a wife named Jalāmbujagarbhā.
Furthermore, O family deity, that Jalāmbujagarbhā had two sons, both boys:
one was named Jalāmbara, and the second was named Jalagarbha.

Then, O lineage deity, Jalavāhana, together with these two boys, the sons of the merchant, traveled by stages through villages, towns, market towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals. Then, O lineage deity, at another time and on another occasion, while on the road, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana reached a certain dense forest wilderness and saw there, along the way, wolves, jackals, crows, and birds that feed on flesh.
They were running toward a direction where, in a wilderness thicket, there was a lotus pond formed by the forest.
Seeing this, it occurred to him:
"For what purpose are these carnivorous wolves, jackals, crows, and birds running in this direction?"
This thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now to go toward that direction,
in which direction these flesh-eaters— the wolves, jackals, crows, and birds— are running?"
Then, O family deity, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana, wandering and strolling along in due course, arrived at the pond situated in the forest.
In that great pond, ten thousand fish were dwelling.
There he saw many hundreds of fish deprived of water, and a heart of compassion arose within him.
There he saw a goddess emerging with half her body visible;
and that goddess said this to the merchant’s son Jalavāhana:
"Excellent, excellent! (Bagchi 99)
"Noble son, you who are named Jalavāhana give water to the fish; for two reasons, O son of good family, you are called 'Water-Bearer':
because you carry water, and because your name corresponds to your deed."
Jalavāhana said,
"O deity, how many fish are these?
The deity replied:
There were ten thousand fish in total.
Then, O Kuladevatā, a supreme mind of compassion arose even more intensely in the merchant’s son Jalavāhana.
At that time, O Kuladevatā, only a small amount of water remained in the lotus pond situated in the wilderness;
those ten thousand fish, deprived of water and having entered the jaws of death, were running about.
Then, O lineage deity, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana ran in the four directions;
in whichever direction the merchant’s son Jalavāhana paced about, in that direction ten thousand fish gazed piteously at Jalavāhana.
Then, O lineage deity, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana ran in the four directions, seeking water;
yet no water was found there at all.
He gazed out in the four directions.
Not far away, he saw a great grove of trees; having climbed that tree and cut off some branches, he went toward the lotus pond.
Having arrived there, he created a very cool shade for those ten thousand fish with the tree branches.

Then, O Kuladevatā, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana searched for the source of the water in that lotus pond, wondering, "From where does the arrival of this water come? He ran in the four directions, yet no water was found.
He followed that stream of water very swiftly, indeed very swiftly.
Furthermore, O family deity, that great river named Jalāgamā, from which water flows into that forest-born lotus pond,

was at that time caused to fall into a great precipice in an unseen place by a certain wicked being for the sake of those ten thousand fish, so that there would be no further arrival of water for those fish.
Seeing that, he thought: "Even by a thousand people, this river cannot be made to flow in that manner; how much less could it be made to flow by me alone? He then turned back.
But indeed, O tutelary deity, the merchant's son Jalavāhana approached very quickly and went to where King Sureśvaraprabha was.
Having approached King Sureśvaraprabha and bowed his head at the king’s feet, he sat down to one side and reported this matter:
"Indeed, Sire, I have pacified the diseases of all beings throughout every village, city, town, district, kingdom, and capital within Your Majesty's realm."
"In that place, there is a lotus pond called Aṭavīsaṃbhavā.
Therein dwell ten thousand fish who have lost their water and are tormented by the sun.
Therefore, may Your Majesty grant me twenty elephants so that I may give life to those beings born in the animal realm."
"Just as it was given and commanded by King Sureśvaraprabha to the men: 'O ministers, give twenty elephants to the Great King of Physicians!
The ministers said:
'Go, O Great Being, to the elephant stable; take possession of the twenty elephants and bring happiness to sentient beings.'"
Then, O Kuladevatā, Jalavāhana, together with his son Jalāmbara, took twenty elephants and received hundreds of leather water-skins from the elephant-keepers.
Having gone to where the great river named Jalāgamā flows,
he filled those skins with water, loaded the water onto the backs of the elephants, and proceeded very swiftly toward the lotus pond situated in the forest.
Having approached, he caused that water to be unloaded from the back of the elephant and filled the lotus pond on all four sides with water; then he walked about on all four sides.
Wherever Jalavāhana walked, there ten thousand fish followed after him.
Then, O Kuladevatā, this thought occurred to Jalavāhana:
"For what reason do these ten thousand fish flee toward where I am?
Furthermore, this thought occurred to him:
"Surely these fish, tormented by the fire of hunger, are seeking food from me;
what if I were to provide them with food?"
Then, O family deity, Jalavāhana spoke thus to his son Jalāmbara:

"Go, noble son, mount the most powerful elephant and proceed very quickly to your own residence. Having approached your grandfather, the merchant, speak to him thus: 'O father, Jalavāhana says this: whatever there is here in the house...'"
"Let there be prepared food for your parents, brothers, sisters, female and male slaves, and laborers;
having gathered it all together in one place, place it upon the back of an elephant and dispatch it very quickly by water-vehicle."

Then the boy Jalāmbara, having mounted the elephant, ran very swiftly toward his own residence; having arrived there, he reported this matter in detail before his grandfather, exactly as previously described.
All of that was then granted by the grandfather to Jalāmbara.
Then the boy Jālambara, having placed that food upon the back of an elephant and mounted the elephant himself, went toward the lotus pond situated in the forest.
Then Jalavāhana, seeing his son Jalāmbara arrive, was thrilled, delighted, and elated; he took food from his son, cut it up, and threw it into that lotus pond.
By that food, those ten thousand fish were fully satisfied.
Again, this thought occurred to him: "I have heard that at another time, in a forest hermitage, a monk who upholds the Mahāyāna said:
'Whoever should hear the name of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaśikhin at the time of his death...'"
"He will be reborn in the heavenly realm.
"What if I were now to teach these fish the profound Dharma of dependent origination,
and cause them to hear the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One?"
And at that time, in this Jambudvīpa, there arose among sentient beings a twofold view:
some had faith in the Mahāyāna, while others reviled it.
Then, at that time, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana, having lowered both his feet knee-deep into that lotus pond, uttered this inspired utterance:
"Homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One! When he was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, he made this vow:
'May whoever in the ten directions, at the time of death, hear my name, upon passing away from there, be reborn in the company of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.'"
(Bagchi 102) Then, indeed, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana taught this Dharma to those beings born in the animal realm:
namely, "from this, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises."
That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces;
conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness;
conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form.
Conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases;
conditioned by the six sense bases is contact;
conditioned by contact is feeling.
With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises.
With existence as condition, birth arises;

with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering, namely: from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
From the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling;
from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging.
From the cessation of clinging, existence ceases;
from the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
from the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"Only the cessation of this great mass of suffering occurs.
Thus, O family deity, at that time and on that occasion, the merchant's son Jalavāhana spoke this Dharma discourse to those who had been born into the animal realm;
together with his two sons, Jalāmbara and Jalagarbha, he returned once more to his own home.
Then, at another time and on another occasion, the merchant’s son Jalavāhana, having enjoyed a great festival and being intoxicated by that great festival, lay down upon his bed.
At that time and on that occasion, a great omen appeared:
when that night had passed, those ten thousand fish died and were reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods in a state of commonality.
As soon as they were born, a reflection such as this arose in their minds:
"By what cause of wholesome karma have we been reborn here among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven? This thought occurred to them.

"In this Jambudvīpa, we were ten thousand fish. Having been born into the animal realm, we were satiated by the merchant’s son Jalavāhana with abundant water and the finest food. Furthermore, the profound Dharma of dependent origination was taught to us."
The name of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaśikhin was made known to them.
By that cause of wholesome dharmas and by that condition, we have been reborn here among the gods.
What if we were now to approach the merchant’s son Jalavāhana?
"Having approached him, we shall pay him honor.
Then those ten thousand sons of the gods vanished from among the Trāyastriṃśa devas and appeared in the house of the merchant Jalavāhana.
At that time, the merchant Jalavāhana was lying upon his couch.
Ten thousand pearl necklaces were placed by those sons of gods upon his head; ten thousand pearl necklaces were placed at the soles of his feet;
and ten thousand pearl necklaces were placed on his right side.
Ten thousand pearl necklaces were placed on the left side;
within the interior of the house, a rain of māndārava flowers fell knee-deep,
and celestial drums resounded.
By means of which all those in Jambudvīpa were awakened;
then the merchant Jalavāhana awoke.
Then those ten thousand sons of gods set out through the path of the sky.

Those sons of gods, showering rains of māndārava flowers here and there throughout the domain of King Sureśvaraprabha, approached the pond situated in the forest. There, in that pond, [they scattered] māndārava flowers.
Then, having showered [rain], they vanished from that very spot and returned once more to the celestial abode;
there they delighted and sported with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
They moved about,
experiencing great glory and good fortune,
and in Jambudvīpa, night turned into dawn.
Then King Sureśvaraprabha asked his astrologers and chief ministers:
"For what reason have these omens appeared tonight?
They replied:
"Your Majesty should know that forty thousand pearl necklaces have rained down upon the merchant's son Jalavāhana, and divine Māndārava flowers are emerging.
The king said:
"Gentlemen, summon the merchant's son Jalavāhana with kind words."
Then those chief ministers and accountants went to the house where Jalavāhana was; having approached him, they said this to the merchant Jalavāhana:
"King Sureśvaraprabha summons you."
Then the merchant Jalavāhana, together with the high ministers, approached King Sureśvaraprabha.
Having approached him, he sat down to one side.
The king asked:

"Jalavāhana, for what reason do you know that such auspicious omens have appeared tonight? Then the merchant Jalavāhana said this to Sureśvaraprabha: 'I know, O Lord, that ten thousand fish have certainly perished.'"
The king asked, "How do you know?
Jalavāhana replied:
"Let Your Majesty go; let Jalāmbara enter that great lotus pond.
Are those ten thousand fish still alive, or have they passed away?
The king said, "So be it."
Then the merchant’s son Jalavāhana said this to the boy Jalāmbara:
"Go, noble son, and look at the lotus pond in the forest;
are those ten thousand fish alive, or have they died?"

Then the boy Jalāmbara went very quickly toward the pond situated in the forest. Having arrived, he saw those ten thousand fish that had died and beheld a great rain of *māndārava* flowers; seeing this, he turned back once more and said this to his father:
"They have passed away.
Then the merchant's son Jalavāhana, having heard these words from the boy Jalambara, went to King Sureśvaraprabha and reported this matter to him.
"Your Majesty should know that those ten thousand fish have all passed away and been reborn among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
It is through the power of those sons of the gods that such auspicious omens have appeared this very night:
forty thousand divine pearl necklaces and celestial māndārava flowers have rained down upon our house."
Then that king became joyful, satisfied, and elated in mind.
Then the Blessed One spoke again to that family deity Bodhisattvasamuccayā as follows:
Furthermore, O Kuladevatā, it might occur to you that at that time, on that occasion, there was another king named Sureśvaraprabha;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?

At that time, on that occasion, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi was the king named Sureśvaraprabha. Furthermore, O Kuladevatā, you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the merchant named Jaṭindhara was someone else;
however, you should certainly not view it in this way.
For what reason?
At that time and on that occasion, King Śuddhodana was the merchant named Jaṭindhara.
"Furthermore, O family deity, you might think that at that time and on that occasion, the merchant's son Jalavāhana was someone else.
But indeed, you should not view it in such a way."
For what reason?
Because at that time, on that occasion, I was the merchant's son Jalavāhana.
Furthermore, O family deity, you might think that at that time and on that occasion, Jalavāhana’s wife named Jalāmbujagarbhā was someone else;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
At that time, on that occasion, the Śākya maiden named Gopā was the wife of Jalavāhana, named Jalāmbujagarbhā. At that time, on that occasion, Rāhulabhadra was a boy named Jalāmbara.
Ānanda, at that time, on that occasion, was a boy named Jalagarbha.
Furthermore, O Kuladevatā, you might think that at that time, on that occasion, those ten thousand fish were someone else;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
For what reason?
Those ten thousand sons of gods, headed by Jvalanāntaratejorāja, were at that time and on that occasion the ten thousand fish whom I satisfied with water and the finest food,
and for whom I taught the profound Dharma of dependent origination.
They were made to hear the name of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaśikhin.
By that cause of wholesome dharmas, they have come here into my presence, and thus they have now received prophecies regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Through extreme joy, serene confidence, gladness, and reverence for hearing the Dharma, they have obtained all these names of prophecy.
Furthermore, O Kuladevatā, you might think that at that time, on that occasion, she was some other tree deity;
it should not be viewed in this way.
And why is that?
O family deity, at that time and at that moment, you were the tree deity.
O family deity, by this analogy it should be understood:
just as many beings have been ripened for enlightenment by me while wandering in saṃsāra.
All of them shall attain the stage of prophecy regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, "The Conversion of Jalavāhana by Means of Fishes," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsottama.
[Chapter on the Tigress]
Furthermore, O deity of the family, one who has become a bodhisattva must even be prepared to sacrifice oneself for the sake of the welfare of others.
How is this so?
Because [the Bodhisattva] possesses the power and prowess of unimpeded wisdom and vision, emitting hundreds of rays of vast, stainless, and manifold virtues that spread throughout heaven and earth.

The Blessed One, surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand monks and endowed with the five kinds of vision, while wandering on a tour through the Pañcāla country, arrived at a certain forest grove.
There he beheld a stretch of ground adorned with various flowers and a surface of soft, green, blue grass; having seen it, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda.
"Ānanda, this spot of earth is beautiful; and in this place, the designation 'the finality' is recognized."
"Now, prepare a seat for the Tathāgata.
Then, at the command of the Blessed One, the seat was prepared.
Having prepared it, he said this to the Blessed One:

“O Blessed One, a seat has been prepared; please sit down, O most venerable, most excellent, best among men, giver of boons, most supreme! Bring forth, for the benefit of humanity, the discourse on the supreme nectar that leads to liberation and is free from death. O Blessed One, [speak] that which is devoid of destruction.
Then the Blessed One, having sat upon that seat, addressed the monks:
“Monks, do you wish to see the bodies of the Bodhisattvas who performed difficult deeds?”
When this had been said, monks, they spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"This is the time, O Best of Sages, to behold the essence of the welfare of beings, which is non-dual and pure as water.
It is fitting for us to open the bones of him who was the locus of immeasurable virtues."

Then the Blessed One struck the surface of the earth with his hand—the palm of which was marked by a thousand-spoked wheel and as soft as a thick, fresh lotus—and at the mere touch, the earth shook in six ways. Thereupon, a stūpa, transformed by the rays of light from his fingernails, rose up from that spot. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda.
"Open this stūpa with joy.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received permission from the Blessed One, opened the stūpa.
There he saw a golden casket covered with pearls spread over it like gold.
Having seen the Blessed One, he said this:
"O Blessed One, a golden water-pot has been recovered.
The Blessed One replied:
"All these seven small seas must be opened.
Then he opened them,
and there he saw bones resembling snow and white water-lilies.
Having seen the Blessed One, he said this to him:
"Blessed One, bones are being perceived.
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, let the relics of the Great Man be brought here."
(Bagchi 107) Then the Venerable Ānanda, having taken those bones, offered them to the Blessed One,
the Buddha. The Blessed One, having accepted the bones, set them down before the Saṅgha and said:

"These are the bones of one who was liberated by the most excellent and supreme qualities; who was further refined by constant and continuous resolve for awakening, firm enthusiasm, fame, self-control, meditation, and patience;
who was steadfast, resolute, and ever devoted to giving.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks," they said, "the relics of the Bodhisattva are perfumed by the virtues of his moral conduct; their sight is extremely difficult to obtain, and they have become a field of merit.
Then those monks, with palms joined and minds deeply moved, bowed their heads in reverence to those relics.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, said this to the Blessed One:

"The Blessed One has arisen above all worlds—past, future, and present—and is honored by all sentient beings; how is it that the Tathāgata himself pays homage to these bones? Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, these bones are worthy of veneration.
For what reason?
Because by means of these very bones, Ānanda, I have thus swiftly awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Long ago, Ānanda, in the past, there was a king named Mahāratha, who possessed vast wealth, grain, vehicles, and military forces, and whose strength and prowess were unimpeded.
He had three sons who resembled celestial youths:
Mahāpraṇāda, Mahādeva, and Mahāsattva.
Then the king went out to a park for the purpose of recreation.
And those princes, drawn by the excellence of that park, wandered here and there with minds eager for flowers, and entered a great thicket in the forest.
When they had dispersed, the attendants of the princes also scattered among one another.
Abandoned by the prince during the great festival of the garden, they entered that thicket of twelve forests unnoticed.
Then Mahāpraṇāda said to his two brothers,
"Fear has entered my heart."
"Come, lest we meet our destruction at the hands of wild beasts.
Mahādeva said:
"I have no fear; rather, it is the separation from my beloved ones that truly agitates my heart."
The Mahāsattva said:
I have neither fear nor sorrow here in this excellent, secluded forest praised by the sages;
rather, the attainment of the most vast and great purpose causes my heart to flourish.

(Bagchi 108) Then those princes, while wandering through that thicket of twelve forest groves, saw a tigress who had given birth seven days prior, surrounded by her five cubs, emaciated by hunger and thirst, and with an exceedingly weak body. Having seen her, they...
Mahāpraṇāda said:
"Alas! This poor woman must have given birth six days ago, or perhaps seven.
Now, failing to obtain food, she will either devour her own children or pass away from hunger."
The Mahāsattva said,
"What is the food of this ascetic woman?
Mahāpraṇāda replied:
If there were here flesh, warm bloods, and substances resembling broth, this would be declared the food of tigers, hyenas, bears, and lions. (Suv 19.3)
Mahādeva said:
"This ascetic woman here, her body overcome by hunger and thirst, possessing only a remnant of life and exceedingly weak, is unable to seek food in any other place.
Who would sacrifice his own life for the sake of preserving hers?"
Mahāpraṇāda said:
"O, the sacrifice of one's own self is difficult to perform!
The Mahāsattva replied:
This method is difficult for those like us who are engaged in the hardships of the body;
it is not difficult for other true persons who are devoted to the welfare of others.
Moreover,
that being who has entered into compassion and pity is found both in heaven and here;
having joyfully offered his own body here hundreds of times for the sake of the bodies of others.
Then those princes, greatly agitated, rushed forward, gazing at her with unblinking eyes, thinking, "This is a tigress! Thereupon, this thought occurred to the Great Being:
"Now is the time for the sacrifice of my own self. Why? Because this body, though cherished for a very long time with costly beds, clothing, food, and vehicles, is now but a putrid thing."

Not abandoning their own inherent nature in successive order until the end, they do not cease being ungrateful, even though they have performed dharmas that bring about the destruction of suffering. (Bagchi 109) Suv_19.6 //
Moreover:
"Since he is the reality existing amidst all seasons, there is nothing for him to depend upon;
having appointed him [to this task], may I become for him a boat for crossing the ocean of old age and death."

Moreover: Having abandoned this body— which is like a mass of excrement, filled with hundreds of births, full of internal filth, as essence-less as foam, and teeming with hundreds of worms— I shall indeed perform my duty.
Free from sorrow, changeless, without substrate, and stainless, complete with qualities such as meditative concentration and wisdom,
I shall attain the utterly pure Dharmakāya, filled with hundreds of virtues.
Having thus resolved and with his heart overcome by supreme compassion, he distracted them, saying:
"May you two go now on your own business; I shall enter the thicket of the twelve forests."
Then that Great Being, the prince, having returned from that grove and approached the dwelling of the tigress, cast his cloak upon a forest creeper and made this vow:

"May I, for the sake of the welfare of the world, awaken to unsurpassed, auspicious enlightenment; and with an unwavering mind, may I compassionately give this body, so difficult for others to abandon.
By that, may I attain that stainless enlightenment which is honored by the sons of the Conquerors—a radiance that shall ferry the three worlds out of the terrifying ocean of existence."
Then the Great Being threw himself down before the tigress. Thereupon, the tigress did nothing at all to the Bodhisattva, who was possessed of loving-kindness.
Then the Bodhisattva, thinking, "This one is weak," rose up and searched for a weapon.
Kṛpāmati did not obtain weapons anywhere;
taking a very strong bamboo pole a hundred years old, he lifted his own son with it and threw himself down near the tigress.
As soon as the Bodhisattva had descended, this earth, like a ship deprived of its course in the midst of the waters, shook in six ways;
it did not shine, like the rays of the sun seized by Rāhu;
and a rain of excellent flowers fell, resting upon divine fragrant powders.
Then another deity, her mind filled with wonder, praised the Bodhisattva.
O wise one, just as your compassion has spread here among sentient beings, so indeed, O hero among men, you cast off this body with joy—
that auspicious and supreme state which is devoid of birth and death.
Before long, you shall attain here that auspicious state which is free from exertion and peaceful.
Then, indeed, that tigress, beholding the Bodhisattva with his body smeared with blood, in a mere moment made him devoid of flesh and blood, leaving only the bones remaining.
Then Mahāpraṇāda, having observed that earthquake, spoke thus to Mahādeva.
The oceans, together with their seas, have begun to tremble; the sun’s rays have fallen asleep across the earth in the ten directions;
a rain of flowers falls in confusion, or rather, my mind is distraught, for my brothers have now surrendered their own bodies here.
Mahādeva said:
"Since he spoke such compassionate words upon seeing her—
who was overcome by hunger, intent on devouring her own offspring, and possessed of a very weak mind beset by hundreds of calamities— my intellect here is indeed filled with doubt."
Then those two princes, overcome by supreme grief and their eyes overflowing with tears, turned back along that path and approached the very vicinity of the tigress.
There they saw a hundred bamboo stakes joined together as a covering, and bones that were dark and discolored, smeared with the mire of blood.
Seeing their hair scattered in various directions and intermediate quarters, the two fainted and fell to the ground;
regaining consciousness after a long time, they rose and, raising their arms, uttered a cry of distress:
"Alas, dear brother! O King! And alas for our mother, who was so devoted to her son!"
That mother will be asked: "Where is the third one among you two, he whose eyes are like lotuses?"
"Alas! Indeed, it would have been more glorious for us to die right here in this very place than to live on.
How could we, deprived of the Great Being, show ourselves to our mother and father?"
Then those two princes, having lamented most variously and piteously, set out.
There, the prince’s attendants, running in every direction and intermediate quarter in search of the prince, saw one another and asked, "Where is the prince? Where is the prince?
At that moment, the queen, lying upon her bed, beheld a dream portending separation from her beloved.
It was as if her breasts were being cut off, as if her teeth were being pulled out, or as if three young doves were being seized—terrified and snatched away by a hawk.
Then the queen, her heart trembling with fear at the shaking of the earth, suddenly woke up and became lost in anxious thought.

"Why does this earth, clothed by the ocean, tremble so violently? Is the sun pierced by a spear, or is some calamity befalling the king? My body suffers pain and my eye throbs; my breast feels as if it were being torn out.
May all be well with my sons who have gone to this forest glade for the sake of sport."
Then, while she was thinking thus, a maidservant entered with a terrified heart and informed the queen:
"My lady, the attendants of the prince are searching for him; it is heard that he has been lost.
Upon hearing that her son had perished, the queen’s heart trembled, and her face and eyes became clouded with tears.
Approaching the king, he said, "Your Majesty, my beloved son is lost; so it is heard.
The king, his heart trembling, fell into a state of extreme terror.
"Alas, what misery! I am separated from my beloved son.
Then the king comforted the queen:
"Do not fear, O Queen; we shall obtain the prince by searching for him."
While the multitude of people was thus engaged, rushing in search of the princes, the king soon thereafter saw from afar two royal princes approaching.
Upon seeing them, the king said, "I have found these two princes, but not all of them."
Alas, what misery is this called separation from one's son!

For those who perceive no [worldly object], there is no such joy as the dejection that men experience from the loss of a son. Indeed, those men are most fortunate whose sons have either met their end through exertion or do not live at all.
Then the queen, overcome by supreme grief, spoke in a piteous voice like a young elephant struck in its vital organs.
If the retinue of the three sons has entered this excellent forest filled with flowers, where is that third son, who is like my own heart; why does he not come here to rescue his younger brother?
When the two of them had arrived, the king, filled with longing, questioned his sons; he asked the princes, "Where is the younger boy?
Thereupon, afflicted by grief, their eyes overflowing with tears, their palates, lips, teeth, and faces parched, they said nothing at all. The queen said:
As they speak, my memory quickly fails and my body is most severely tormented.
Where is that son of mine, my third heart? This very heart is bursting or fainting away.
Then those two princes related that event in detail.
Upon hearing it, the king, the queen, and the attendants fell into a swoon.
When they had recovered from their fainting, they went to that place, weeping with voices choked by piteous grief.
Then the king and the queen, seeing those bones— devoid of blood and flesh, scattered in all directions and intermediate points by the wind like disheveled hair—

fell to the ground like trees struck down. Thereupon, the domestic priest, having beheld that state for a very long time, refreshed the bodies of the king and the queen with water and the paste of *malaya* sandalwood.
Then, after a long time, having regained consciousness, the king rose and lamented most piteously.
Alas, what misery! O son, where have you gone? You, so full of desire and beautiful to behold, have so quickly fallen under the power of death.
For once you have reached the very jaws of death, there will be no other sorrow for me greater than this.

And the queen, overcome by delusion, with her hair disheveled, beating her breast with both arms, rolls upon the surface of the earth like a fish leaping from its place; she weeps most piteously like a queen who has lost her calf, or like a female elephant whose young has perished.
"Alas, beloved! Dear son, where are you going? This lotus has indeed been broken and scattered upon the surface of the earth.
By what enemy on this earth has my son been destroyed today—he who was a moon enchanting to the eyes?
Alas, why does my body not shatter here today? I see my excellent son slain upon the ground!"
"Clearly my heart is made of stone, for it does not break upon seeing this calamity—alas, this evil fruit of a dream! For today these two breasts have been severed by someone with a sword;
and in another dream, my beloved son was quickly destroyed after his two tusks were torn out."
Just as he was carried off by a hawk here with my three captured pigeons,
so today, though surrounded by his three sons, he alone has been slain by death.
(Bagchi 114) Then the king and the queen, lamenting most piteously in many ways, removed all their ornaments and,
together with a great multitude of people, performed the funeral rites for their son’s body at that spot on earth where there were golden stūpas.
Those bodies were laid down.
Furthermore, Ānanda, you might think that at that time and on that occasion, the prince named Mahāsattva was someone else;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
And why is that?
At that time, on that occasion, I was the prince named Mahāsattva.

Even then, Ānanda, though I was not yet free from hatred and delusion toward kings, I favored the world out of compassion so that it might be spared from the sufferings of the hells and other realms. How much more so now, when I am a perfectly awakened Buddha, entirely free from all faults?
"For indeed, for the sake of each and every sentient being, I would endure birth in the hells for an eon so as to liberate them from saṃsāra;
yet the world is sustained by the very essence of sentient beings, and this task is difficult, manifold, and diverse."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
For many eons, seeking this supreme enlightenment, I have sacrificed my own self;
just as one might sacrifice for a king, so too have I sacrificed my very bodies for the sake of the prince.
I recall that in former births there was a king named Mahāratha;
he too had two sons who were great in renunciation, and the elder among them was named Mahāsattva.
He then had two brothers named Mahādeva and Mahāpraṇāda;
having gone to a forest thicket with those of their own clan, they saw a tigress overcome by hunger.
Born of compassion for that supreme being, he thought: "What if I were to give up my own flesh?
For this tigress, tormented by hunger and thirst, would otherwise devour her own offspring. (Suv 19.26)
Then that great being, the son of a great chariot-warrior,
fell down upon seeing the tigress afflicted by hunger, for the sake of liberating her cubs.

When he, who consists of compassion, fell upon this earth, the ground with its mountains trembled; the flocks of birds fled in various directions, the herds of deer were terrified, and this world became agitated and distressed.
His two brothers, Mahāpraṇāda and Mahādeva,
did not find that Great Being while they were in this great forest tract.
With hearts pierced by the arrow of excessive grief, they wander through the forest depths unconscious;
seeking their brother, they roam the middle of the woods with faces like those of donkeys.
Both those princes, Mahāpraṇāda and Mahādeva,
approached that place where the very weak tigress lay with her cubs.
Seeing his limbs smeared with blood, scattered upon the earth as mere hair, bones, and skin,
they see whatever small portion of him has fallen to the ground.
(Bagchi 116) Both those princes fell there upon the earth in a swoon;
their minds were lost, their bodies smeared with dust, and they were bewildered, deprived of memory and their senses. (Suv_19.33)
And their attendants, weeping with piteous voices and afflicted by grief,
raised their many arms and cried out as they sprinkled him with water.
As soon as he had fallen into it, she, along with her attendants and her chief queen who was displeasing to him,
saw herself within the royal palace, having entered it easily surrounded by five hundred women.
From those two breasts, milk flowed forth in streams; for even though her entire body was being pierced as if by needles, she let it flow with great force.

With a heart reeling from extreme grief, pierced by the arrows of sorrow for her son’s separation, she approached the king with a deeply dejected mind, tormented by intense anguish; weeping in a piteous voice, she then spoke to the great chariot-warrior, the king: Suv_19.37.
Listen to me, O King, lord of men: my body is being consumed by the fire of grief;
from both my breasts, milk has been released in an instant.
They tormented my limbs one by one as if with needles, and my very heart;
such was the omen that I shall no longer behold the sight of my beloved sons. (Suv 19.39)
"O wise one, grant me life for my sons; bring me security!
I have seen a dream: three young pigeons were mine, and of these, I am deeply attached to the third young pigeon. (Suv 19.40)
A hawk entered there, and a dove was carried off by the hawk; even in my dreams, such grief as this has entered this heart of mine.
"Excessive burning, grief, and anxiety will bring about my death before long;
O sons, understand this! Grant me my life through your own compassion."
Having spoken thus, the chief queen fainted and fell there upon the ground, deprived of mindfulness, her mind destroyed, and her consciousness lost;
and all those in the inner apartments wept with piteous voices, crying out in lamentation.
Seeing that chief queen fallen there upon the ground in a swoon,
the lord of kings, afflicted by immediate grief at the separation from his sons, was accompanied by his ministers;
and the ministers were dispatched, having gone out for the purpose of seeking the princes.
(118) All the people within the city, having risen up and seized various weapons, came forth with tearful faces and, weeping, asked that Great Being on the roads: *Suv_19.45*
Is he still alive? Where has that Great Being gone now? Shall I see today that beloved being, so dear to behold, whose fatigue has not yet been dispelled? (Suv 19.46)
With a sorrowful face and making a terrible sound of lamentation, Ghoṣa wanders through this realm amidst the perils of endless toil; the king, a great chariot-warrior, rises up weeping.

Afflicted with grief, he sprinkles streams of water upon the chief queen as she falls to the ground; he sprinkles her with water until she regains consciousness, and having risen, she asks with a dejected mind: Suv_19.48.

"Are my sons indeed dead, or do they live? So too, the king, the great chariot-warrior, and the chief queen? Thus did the ministers and courtiers speak in every direction and intermediate quarter, having gone out for the purpose of inquiry.
"O princes, do not let your minds become overly dejected, nor let your hearts be overcome by grief for one who has passed away.
Having thus obtained forgiveness from the Great Charioteer and the Chief Queen, Kampa then departed."
Then, with a face bathed in tears, weeping and afflicted by grief, surrounded by a host of ministers,
he departed from the royal palace with a deeply dejected mind and downcast eyes, going out before the city for the sake of inquiry.
(Bagchi 119) With his face covered in tears, the king ran about weeping for his many sons.
Seeing that the king had departed, he followed closely behind him and immediately went out as well. // Suv_19.52 //
Immediately thereafter, that king, a great chariot-warrior, looked about in order to see his beloved son;
with eyes well-composed, he gazed in all directions and saw a certain man with a shaven head.
With limbs smeared with blood and a body covered in dust, he went along weeping with a tearful face;
afflicted by terrible grief, he stood in the heart of the great chariot-warrior, weeping with a tearful face.

Standing with his arms raised and wailing, one of the ministers then arrived in haste; approaching quickly from afar, they spoke to the king, the great chariot-warrior: Suv_19.55. "O King, Great Charioteer! they said.
"Do not be sorrowful in heart, O King; your sons remain dear and pleasing to you.
Before long, having returned here to your presence, you shall behold that most excellent and beloved son."
After he had departed for only a moment, the king’s second minister arrived;
covered in dust, clad in soiled garments, and with a tearful face, he spoke thus to the king:
O great king of men, your two other sons remain here, set ablaze by the fire of grief;
yet your one excellent son is not seen, O King, for that Great Being has been seized by impermanence.
And having seen a tigress who had recently given birth and was intent on devouring her own cubs, that Great Being, the noble youth, generated a great force of compassion for them. (Suv 19.59)
Having made a sublime vow for enlightenment, [I thought: "I shall awaken all sentient beings here;
having sought that profound and sublime enlightenment, may I realize it in a future age."

The Great Being fell upon the edge of the mountain slope; standing there before the tigress who was overcome by hunger, the prince, in a mere moment, was made fleshless, his limbs reduced until only bones remained.
And having heard these words, which were like nectar, that king and great chariot-warrior fainted;
he fell to the earth, his mind destroyed, blazing with a most terrible fire of grief.
The ministers and courtiers, weeping with piteous voices and afflicted by grief, sprinkled him with water;
all stood with their arms upraised, wailing, as the third minister spoke to the king.
"Today, I saw both princes there in this great forest;
they had fallen upon the earth with their minds lost, and we sprinkled them with water."
As soon as they regain their mindfulness while remaining there, they see the four directions ablaze;
they stand for a moment and then fall to the ground, lamenting with piteous cries.
(Bagchi 121) They stood constantly with arms upraised, uttering the praises of those two brothers;
and that king, too, was dejected at heart, his mind utterly distraught by the separation from his sons.
Overwhelmed by grief and lamenting, the king indeed wailed thus:
"My only son, dear and pleasing to me, my youngest, has been seized by a forest-rākṣasa."
"Let not these two sons of mine, nor any others, meet with the destruction of their lives through the fire of grief.
What if I were now to go there quickly, so that I might see those two sons of lovely appearance?"
Let him enter the royal capital by a swift vehicle and quickly reach the inner palace;
lest she, desiring to give birth, have her heart shattered by the fire of grief.
Seeing his two sons, he attained peace; he did not suffer the loss of their lives.
And the king, together with his assembly of ministers, mounted upon an elephant, went there to see them.
Seeing his two sons crying out with piteous voices, calling for their brothers, the king, though filled with grief,
took those two sons and, weeping himself, entered the city.
Hurrying as fast as possible, he beheld his queen, who longed for her sons, together with her children.
And I myself was formerly that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the most excellent of Great Beings.
And he was the son of that great chariot-warrior king, by whom the tigress had been made happy.
For Śuddhodana was indeed the excellent lord of kings, a king named Mahāratha;
his queen was the excellent Māyādevī, and likewise Maitrīya was the Mahāpraṇāda.
Then there was a great queen; the prince Mañjuśrī became the heroic Kumārabhūta;
Mahāprajāpatī became the tigress there, and these five monks were indeed her tiger cubs.

Then the Great King and the Great Queen, having uttered various lamentations of compassion and spoken these words of mourning, together with a great multitude of people, performed the funeral rites for their son; in this place, the relics of that Mahāsattva were enshrined within this stūpa made of the seven precious gems.
There, the Great Being, the Deva, relinquished his own body to this tigress; and out of compassion, he made such a vow:
"By means of this dedication of my body, in a future time, after incalculable eons, may I bring about the Buddha-body for all sentient beings."

While this teaching was being expounded, the minds of immeasurable beings— including gods and humans— were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This is the cause and this is the condition for the manifestation of this stūpa here.
And that stūpa, through the Buddha’s supernatural empowerment, vanished right there.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Tigress," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
(Bagchi 123) // The Chapter on the Praise of All Tathāgatas //

Then, indeed, those many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas approached the Tathāgata Suvarṇaratnākaracchatrakūṭa. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of that Tathāgata Suvarṇaratnākaracchatrakūṭa and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence, desiring to praise that Tathāgata Suvarṇaratnākaracchatrakūṭa.
Golden-hued, with a body never forsaken, golden-hued, with limbs radiantly illuminated;
golden-hued like a mountain, O Lord of Munis, golden-hued, O Lotus among Munis.
His limbs were adorned with the primary marks and beautified by the secondary characteristics; his body was variegated with exquisite minor marks.
He shone with the brilliant luster of refined gold, utterly stainless and serene like the king of mountains.
Brahmeśvara, with the beautiful resonance of Brahmā’s voice; Siṃheśvara, with a roar like the sound of thunderclouds;
and Aṅgavaccātasvaranirmaleśvara, with a voice like the song of the peacock and the kalaviṅka bird. Suv_20.3.
The Sun, most pure and stainless, possessing beautiful radiance, adorned with a hundred marks of merit;
the Sun, an ocean of utter purity and stainlessness, the Sun, honored by all the hosts of Mount Sumeru.
He who has supreme compassion for the welfare of living beings, the supreme bestower of happiness upon the worlds,
the excellent teacher of the ultimate truth, the Lord who grants the bliss of final nirvāṇa.
The giver of the nectar of happiness, possessing the power of loving-kindness and vigor, and endowed with skillful means—
it would not be possible, even in hundreds of millions of billions of kalpas as numerous as the Ganges sands or the great oceans, to reveal even a single one of your qualities.
This brief [teaching], arising from the ocean of the *Guṇabindu*, has been revealed by me;
by whatever accumulation of merit has been gathered through it, may all beings attain supreme enlightenment.

Then the bodhisattva Ruciraketu rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, at that moment praised him with these verses:
O Lord of Munis, you who possess the marks of a hundred merits, adorned with a thousand beautiful qualities of glory,
O you of noble complexion and most gentle appearance, you are born like the sun with its thousand rays.
Its radiance is agitated by the swirling of many rays, resembling a mass of various jewels;
it has the luster of blue, white, dark, and golden hues, and the brilliance of beryl, copper, gold, crystal, and agate.
"You do not shine like Mount Meru with infinite millions of playful rays of light;
be gracious to me, for you, who move for the happiness of sentient beings, cause even Indra and the fierce sun to be scorched."
With clear complexion and senses, beautiful to behold, with a form that inspires fervor and a form of great loveliness;
possessing an unprecedented color, O Hero, O Radiant One, you shine like a liberated [jewel] with the luster of a swarm of bees.
Adorned with the qualities of pure compassion, accumulated through the merit of equal power of loving-kindness,
honored by various and complete secondary marks, and embellished by the virtues of the concentrations and factors of enlightenment.
For by you, who bring delight, who bring happiness, and who are the source of auspiciousness and the arrival of all the mines of bliss—
you who are adorned with diverse and profound qualities— you shine forth across thousands of millions of buddha-fields.
O Hero, you shine like the sun with its rays; as the orb of the sun in the sky, and as Mount Meru endowed with all virtues, you are seen throughout all the realms of the three worlds.
Resembling cow’s milk, a conch shell, a white lotus, and the moon, with a radiance as pale-white as frost or a white lotus,
a row of tusks shines from your mouth, filling the sky like a flight of swans.
Resting within the interior of your gentle moon-like face, curling to the right,
it shines like the sun in the sky with the rays of light from its hair-tufts, which have the color of lapis lazuli gems.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Praise of All Tathāgatas," in the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Exalted Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
(Bagchi 126) // The Chapter on the Conclusion //
Then, indeed, the family deity named Bodhisattvasamuccayā, joyful and satisfied, at that moment praised the Blessed One with these verses:
Homage be to the Buddha, whose awakening is perfectly pure; to him who has awakened to the manifestation of the pure Dharma;
to him who has awakened to the attainment of the merit of the True Dharma; to the one whose awakening is pure and for whom even the peak of existence is empty.
Aho! Aho! The Buddha’s mind is unassailable; aho! aho! it is equal to the ocean and Mount Meru.
Aho! aho! the Buddha’s infinite range is as exceedingly rare as the flower of the udumbara tree.
Oh, oh! How compassionate is the Tathāgata, the banner of the Śākya clan and the sun among kings, by whom this supreme sūtra has been spoken for the sake of favoring all sentient beings!
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Lord of Peace and supreme among beings, has entered the City of Peace;
he is the profound teacher, the hero who has entered the meditative absorption that is the domain of the Buddhas.
The bodies of the śrāvakas are empty, and the dwellings of the supreme among bipeds are empty;
all those phenomena are empty by their very nature, and even a sentient being, a self, or a person is not found.

Constantly and evermore I remember the sight of the Lord; constantly and evermore I grieve for the lack of his vision. And I perpetually and evermore make this aspiration for the sake of beholding the Buddha, the Sun. (Suv_21.6)
Having established [the Buddha] here eternally upon the earth, I am tormented by exceeding grief at not seeing the Lord;
I weep because of the state of being without a compassionate leader, and I am intensely longing to see the Sugata.
I am constantly and utterly consumed on all sides by the fire of grief; sprinkle upon me the cooling water of your sight!
May the beings who thirst for the vision of your form refresh me with the water of your compassion.
O Leader, show compassion toward me; grant me a vision of your gentle form!
For by you, O Savior, the medicine has been taught, as well as the emptiness of the body and likewise of the disciples.
Equal to space and having the nature of the sky, they are like an illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water;
all sentient beings are of the nature of a dream, a great emptiness, and belong to the Great Leader himself.
Then the Blessed One, rising from his seat, spoke with a Brahma-voice:
"Excellent, excellent, O tutelary deity! The Teacher grants you 'well done. Excellent, O tutelary deity! And again, 'well done'!"
The Blessed One spoke thus, and those bodhisattvas— headed by the bodhisattva Samuccaya, the local deities, and the great goddess Sarasvatī—
as well as that entire assembly, headed by gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Conclusion," of the Sovereign King of Sutras, the Glorious Suvarṇaprabhāsottama.
Thus ends the noble and glorious Suvarṇaprabhāsottama, the king of the sovereign sūtras.
